items.stem: A 0.4 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness 100 N m⁻¹. It then oscillates vertically with amplitude 0.024 m, where g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the static equilibrium extension Δx_eq of the spring?
items.workedSolution: At static equilibrium, upward spring tension balances weight: k Δx_eq = mg ⇒ Δx_eq = (0.4 × 9.8) / 100 = 0.0392 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Hooke's law as k / (mg) instead of mg / k.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds the oscillation amplitude x₀ to mg / k, finding maximum total stretch rather than static equilibrium extension.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides mass m directly by spring constant k without multiplying by gravitational field strength g.

items.stem: A 0.8 kg mass oscillates in SHM with ω = 10 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 0.06 m. A sensor monitors the mass at x = 0.048 m. Calculate the frequency f_E at which its kinetic energy oscillates.
items.workedSolution: Mechanical frequency f = ω / (2π) = 10 / (2π) = 1.592 Hz. Because kinetic energy reaches a maximum twice per mechanical period, f_E = 2f = ω / π = 3.18 Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates 2ω in rad s⁻¹ without dividing by 2π to convert to hertz.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Gives the mechanical displacement frequency f = ω / (2π) instead of recognizing that E_k ∝ cos²(ωt) oscillates at 2f.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Halves the mechanical frequency instead of doubling it.

items.stem: A refracting telescope is set up in normal adjustment. Its objective lens has focal length 2.40 m and its eyepiece lens has focal length 0.040 m.
items.workedSolution: (a) $M = \frac{2.40}{0.040} = 60.0$. (b) $L = 2.40 + 0.040 = 2.44 m$. (c) The observer views a virtual inverted image formed at infinity.

markScheme.criterion: States $L = f_o + f_e$ for normal adjustment.
States the image is virtual and inverted.
States the final image is formed at infinity.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular magnification of the telescope in normal adjustment.
Calculate the separation between the objective and eyepiece lenses.
workingSteps: In normal adjustment the principal foci coincide: $L = f_o + f_e$.

parts.prompt: State the nature and location of the final image viewed by an observer with a relaxed eye.
parts.expectedAnswer: The final image is a virtual inverted image formed at infinity.
workingSteps: Rays emerge parallel from the eyepiece after passing through the inverted real intermediate image.
Hence the observer sees a virtual, inverted image at infinity.

items.stem: The graph shows acceleration against displacement for an object in SHM. It oscillates at 4 Hz with amplitude 0.03 m. Using a = −ω²x, calculate the signed acceleration at x = -0.0225 m.
items.workedSolution: Angular frequency ω = 2πf = 2π(4) = 25.13 rad s⁻¹. By the defining SHM equation, a = −ω²x = −(25.13)²(-0.0225) = 14.2 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ω = 2πf and obtains 14.2 m s⁻² (D).

options.distractorRationale: Substitutes cyclic frequency f directly for angular frequency ω, computing −f²x instead of −(2πf)²x.

items.stem: A short light pulse enters a 1800 m step-index optical fibre (core index 1.55, cladding index 1.47). The end sits in air (n_ext = 1.00), with a 11.8° ray shown, and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Calculate the modal delay Δt = t_max − t_axial at the exit.
items.workedSolution: Axial transit time t_min = n_core L / c = (1.55 × 1800) / (3.00 × 10⁸) = 9.30 × 10⁻⁶ s. At the critical angle sin θ_c = n_clad / n_core, t_max = t_min / sin θ_c = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 9.81 × 10⁻⁶ s. Modal delay Δt = t_max − t_min = 5.06 × 10⁻⁷ s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δt = (n_core L / c)(n_core / n_clad − 1) = 5.06 × 10⁻⁷ s (C).

items.stem: An 80 m step-index optical fibre has a glass core (n_core = 1.62) and cladding (n_clad = 1.51). Light enters from air (n_ext = 1.00) at 12.6° to the axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) sin θ_c = 1.51 / 1.62 ⇒ θ_c = 68.8°. (b) By Snell's law at the end-face, sin θ_axis = (1 sin 12.6°) / 1.62, so θ_axis = 7.74°. (c) Wall incident angle θ_w = 90° − θ_axis = 82.3°, which exceeds θ_c so the ray is guided by TIR.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts θ_axis from 90° to obtain θ_w.

parts.prompt: Calculate the critical angle θ_c at the core–cladding interface.
Calculate the angle θ_axis that the refracted ray inside the core makes with the central axis.
workingSteps: n_ext sin θ_in = n_core sin θ_axis ⇒ sin θ_axis = (1 × sin 12.6°) / 1.62.

parts.prompt: Determine the angle of incidence θ_w of this ray on the core–cladding wall normal, confirming that total internal reflection occurs.

items.stem: Light of vacuum wavelength 450 nm passes from air (n₁ = 1) into diamond (n₂ = 2.42). It hits the flat boundary at 22° to the normal, with vacuum speed 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Calculate its wavelength in diamond.
items.workedSolution: Wave frequency remains unchanged across the boundary, while phase speed decreases to v₂ = c / n₂. Hence λ₂ = λ₀ / n₂ = 450 / 2.42 = 186 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ₂ = λ₀ / n₂ = 450 / 2.42 to obtain 186 nm (B).

items.stem: An upright object of height h_o = 0.02 m stands at u = 0.08 m in front of a thin diverging lens. Its focal length is f = −0.1 m in the real-is-positive sign convention.
items.workedSolution: (a) Optical power P = 1 / (−0.1) = -10.0 D. (b) 1/v = −1/0.1 − 1/0.08 ⇒ v = -0.0444 m. (c) Axial separation between object and virtual image on the same side = u − |v| = 0.0356 m.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes f = −0.1 m and u = 0.08 m into 1/v = 1/f − 1/u.
Subtracts |v| from u because virtual image and object are on the same side of the lens.

Calculate the signed image distance v using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.
Determine the axial distance between the object and its virtual image.
workingSteps: Both lie on the input side of the lens, so separation = u − |v| = |u + v| = 0.0356 m.

items.stem: A 0.2 kg mass is hung on a vertical spring of stiffness 64 N m⁻¹ and moves in vertical SHM of amplitude 0.042 m. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Find the equilibrium extension Δx_eq from the unstretched length.
items.workedSolution: At static equilibrium, upward spring tension balances weight: k Δx_eq = mg ⇒ Δx_eq = (0.2 × 9.81) / 64 = 0.0307 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds the oscillation amplitude x₀ to mg / k, finding maximum total stretch rather than static equilibrium extension.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides mass m directly by spring constant k without multiplying by gravitational field strength g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Hooke's law as k / (mg) instead of mg / k.

items.stem: An undamped mass–spring oscillator completes one full simple harmonic oscillation of period $T$ as shown in the energy graphs. Which statement accurately describes the energy transfers during one cycle?
items.workedSolution: Energy exchanges continuously between E_k and E_p twice per mechanical cycle (at frequency 2f) while their sum E_T remains constant. Therefore the correct statement is: Kinetic energy is maximum at equilibrium and zero at amplitude extremes while potential energy peaks twice per cycle and total energy remains constant.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: kinetic energy is maximum at equilibrium and zero at amplitude extremes while potential energy peaks twice per cycle and total energy remains constant.

options.label: A
options.text: Kinetic energy reaches its maximum value once per oscillation at one amplitude extreme while total energy oscillates sinusoidally.
options.distractorRationale: Kinetic energy peaks twice per cycle (passing equilibrium in both directions), and total energy stays constant.

options.label: B
options.text: Potential energy is maximum at the equilibrium position where the mass moves fastest.
options.distractorRationale: At equilibrium displacement x = 0 so potential energy is minimum and kinetic energy is maximum.

options.label: C
options.text: Kinetic energy and potential energy reach their maximum values simultaneously at the midpoint of the motion.
options.distractorRationale: Since E_k + E_p = E_T (constant), kinetic energy is maximum precisely when potential energy is zero.

options.label: D
options.text: Kinetic energy is maximum at equilibrium and zero at amplitude extremes while potential energy peaks twice per cycle and total energy remains constant.

items.stem: A light ray in water (refractive index 1.33) enters a straight 300 m optical fibre at 14.7° to the axis. The fibre has n_core = 1.58 and n_clad = 1.49. Calculate the total path length of the ray through the 300 m fibre.
items.workedSolution: Inside the core, sin θ_axis = (1.33 sin 14.7°) / 1.58 ⇒ θ_axis = 12.3°. The total zig-zag geometric path length is L_ray = L / cos θ_axis = 300 / cos 12.33° = 307 m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds θ_axis = 12.3° and computes L / cos θ_axis = 307 m (B).

items.stem: An object of height 0.015 m is viewed through a thin convex lens of focal length 0.25 m. Its virtual image forms 0.531 m in front of the lens (v = −0.531 m). Calculate the object distance u.
items.workedSolution: For a virtual image in the real-is-positive convention, v = -0.531 m. Thus 1/u = 1/f − 1/v = 1/0.25 − (1/-0.5313) = 5.882 m⁻¹, giving u = 0.170 m.

items.stem: A narrow light ray in water (n₀ = 1.33) passes through a flat zircon block (n₁ = 1.92, thickness 0.03 m). It enters at 26° to the normal and exits back into water. Find the lateral displacement of the emerging ray.
items.workedSolution: By Snell's law, sin θ₁ = (1.33 sin 26°) / 1.92 ⇒ θ₁ = 17.7°. The perpendicular lateral displacement of the emergent ray is d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.00456 m.

items.stem: A light ray travels inside diamond (n₁ = 2.42) and hits a flat boundary with ethanol (n₂ = 1.36). The angle of incidence is 51° to the normal, and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Through what angle does the ray turn from its original path?
items.workedSolution: Since sin θ_c = 1.36 / 2.42 gives θ_c = 34.2° and θ₁ = 51° > θ_c, total internal reflection occurs with θ_r = 51°. The angular deviation from the original forward direction is δ = 180° − 2(51°) = 78.0°.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies TIR (θ₁ > θ_c = 34.2°) and computes δ = 180° − 2θ₁ = 78.0° (A).

items.stem: A pendulum bob of mass m = 0.5 kg hangs from a light string of length L = 1.9 m. It swings in small-angle SHM with arc amplitude x₀ = 0.475 m. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) T = 2π√(1.9 / 9.81) = 2.77 s. (b) v_max = √(9.81 / 1.9) × 0.475 = 1.08 m s⁻¹. (c) Lowest-point cord tension = m(g + v_max² / L) = 5.21 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies v_max = ω x₀ = (2π / T) x₀.
Uses T_cord = mg + mv_max² / L at the bottom of the arc.

Calculate the maximum speed v_max of the bob as it passes through equilibrium.
Determine the tension in the suspension cord as the bob passes through its lowest point.

items.stem: The graph plots kinetic energy Eₖ, potential energy Eₚ, and total mechanical energy Eₜₒₜ against time t over one full oscillation period T of an undamped oscillator. Which description of the energy–time curves is correct?
items.workedSolution: Since cos²(ωt) = ½(1 + cos 2ωt) and sin²(ωt) = ½(1 − cos 2ωt), both energy curves oscillate at frequency 2f with period T/2. Therefore the correct statement is: As energy exchanges continuously without damping, kinetic energy and potential energy each oscillate between zero and the constant total energy twice per full cycle with period T/2 and frequency 2f.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: kinetic energy and potential energy each oscillate between zero and the constant total energy twice per full cycle with period T/2 and frequency 2f.

items.stem: Even in a narrow single-mode fibre, a white-light pulse broadens because red and violet wavelengths have different refractive indices in silica glass. How is material dispersion eliminated?
items.workedSolution: Material dispersion is caused by wavelength-dependent speed $v = c/n(\lambda)$, mitigated by using monochromatic light (e.g. a narrow-band laser). Therefore option D is correct: use monochromatic light so all waves travel at the same speed in the core.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: use monochromatic light so all waves travel at the same speed in the core.

items.stem: In the displacement-time graph of free damped systems, what uniquely distinguishes critical damping from both light damping and heavy damping?
items.workedSolution: By definition, a critically damped oscillator returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating. Therefore the correct statement is: A critically damped oscillator returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating.

options.label: A
options.text: A critically damped oscillator returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating

options.label: B
options.text: A critically damped oscillator completes exactly one full overshoot cycle before stopping.
options.distractorRationale: Mistakenly allows one overshoot cycle in critical damping.

options.label: C
options.text: A critically damped oscillator takes the longest possible time to return without oscillating.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses heavy overdamping with critical damping.

options.label: D
options.text: A critically damped oscillator maintains constant amplitude while oscillating at its natural frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Describes an undamped free oscillator.

items.stem: Engineers test a tall steel building frame on a horizontal shake table. They measure the sway amplitude and phase lag across a range of ground frequencies before and after adding viscous dampers.
items.workedSolution: Adding dampers lowers the peak amplitude, broadens the resonance peak, and shifts the peak frequency slightly below the natural frequency. Damaging resonance occurs when the ground driving frequency matches the building's natural frequency f₀, giving the fastest energy transfer into the frame. Viscous dampers transfer vibrational energy to thermal energy each cycle, lowering amplitude at every frequency, broadening the peak, and shifting it below f₀. Well below f₀ the frame moves in phase with the ground (0 rad lag); at f = f₀ it lags by π/2 rad (90°); well above f₀ it moves in antiphase (π rad lag).

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Identifies resonance when ground driving frequency matches the skyscraper's natural frequency f₀.
L1b: Explains that at resonance the rate of energy transfer into structural oscillations is maximised.
L2a: Explains that dampers dissipate mechanical energy to thermal energy each cycle, lowering amplitude at all frequencies and broadening the peak.
L2b: Correctly states that adding damping shifts the peak frequency slightly below f₀.
L3a: States phase lag behind the driver is ~0 rad well below f₀ and π/2 rad (90°) at f = f₀.
L3b: States phase lag approaches π rad (180°, antiphase) well above f₀, explaining high-frequency inertial lag.

Well below f₀ the frame moves in phase with the ground (0 rad lag); at f = f₀ it lags by π/2 rad (90°); well above f₀ it moves in antiphase (π rad lag).

items.stem: The displacement–time graph compares three free damping regimes (curves A, B, and C) for a vehicle suspension spring. In each case, the unit is pushed downwards and released from rest.
items.workedSolution: Critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating, while heavy damping returns more slowly. Curve A shows light damping: the oscillator makes repeated cycles of nearly constant period while drag transfers mechanical energy to thermal energy, so peak amplitude decays exponentially. Curve B shows critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating or overshooting. Curve C shows heavy overdamping: large viscous drag causes a slow return to equilibrium without oscillating. Car shock absorbers aim for critical damping so tyres regain road grip quickly after a bump without bouncing or staying compressed.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Correctly identifies light damping (curve A) as oscillating with exponentially decaying amplitude and approximately constant period.
L1b: Explains that resistive damping forces do work to transfer mechanical energy into thermal energy in the damper/surroundings.
L2a: Defines critical damping (curve B) as returning to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating/overshooting.
L2b: Distinguishes heavy/overdamping (curve C) as returning to equilibrium without oscillating but taking significantly longer than critical damping.
L3a: Justifies critical damping for car suspension so wheels return rapidly to normal position after a bump for safe tyre grip.
L3b: Explains why light damping causes uncomfortable/unsafe repeated bouncing whereas heavy damping leaves suspension sluggish over consecutive bumps.

parts.prompt: Identify and compare the behaviour of light damping, critical damping, and heavy overdamping. Explain the energy transfer that reduces the amplitude in light damping. Justify why car shock absorbers are designed close to critical damping.
parts.expectedAnswer: Critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating, while heavy damping returns more slowly. Curve A shows light damping: the oscillator makes repeated cycles of nearly constant period while drag transfers mechanical energy to thermal energy, so peak amplitude decays exponentially. Curve B shows critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating or overshooting. Curve C shows heavy overdamping: large viscous drag causes a slow return to equilibrium without oscillating. Car shock absorbers aim for critical damping so tyres regain road grip quickly after a bump without bouncing or staying compressed.
workingSteps: Contrast light (exponential oscillating decay), critical (fastest non-oscillatory return), and heavy (slow non-oscillatory return) regimes.
Connect amplitude decay to dissipative drag transferring mechanical energy into thermal energy.
Justify critical damping in vehicle suspension for rapid road-grip recovery without bounce.

items.stem: An undamped mass–spring system is pulled to x = +A and released from rest at t = 0. Its motion obeys x = A cos(ωt), as shown in the graphs.
items.workedSolution: undamped simple harmonic motion obeys x = A cos(omega t), linking sinusoidal displacement, velocity, and acceleration curves via quarter-cycle phase shifts and gradients while kinetic and potential energy exchange at twice the oscillation frequency. Starting from x = +A at t = 0, displacement follows a cosine curve x = A cos(ωt). Velocity is the gradient of x–t, giving v = −v_max sin(ωt) with v_max = ωA, leading displacement by π/2 rad (a quarter period) so speed peaks at x = 0 (T/4 and 3T/4) and is zero at ±A. Acceleration is the gradient of v–t and obeys a = −ω²x, so a–t is an inverted cosine in antiphase (π rad) with x–t, peaking at ±ω²A at the extremes. Potential energy E_p = ½mω²x² peaks at 0, T/2, T while kinetic energy E_k peaks at T/4, 3T/4; both stay non-negative and oscillate at frequency 2f (period T/2) while E_k + E_p = E_tot stays constant.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Identifies x = A cos(ωt) starting at +A at t = 0 and correctly states a = −ω²x.
L1: Links velocity to the gradient of the x–t graph and acceleration to the gradient of the v–t graph.
L2: States exact π/2 rad (quarter-period) phase difference between v and x, with v = 0 at ±A and v_max = ωA at equilibrium.
L2: States exact π rad antiphase relationship between a and x, with a = 0 at equilibrium and a_max = ω²A at ±A.
L3: Explains that E_k and E_p are always non-negative and exchange smoothly so E_tot = E_k + E_p = ½mω²A² stays constant.
L3: Explicitly explains why E_k and E_p complete two cycles per oscillation (period T/2, frequency 2f), peaking twice per period.

parts.prompt: Explain how the x–t, v–t, a–t, and energy–time graphs relate over one full period T. Include phase differences, gradients, maxima, and the energy oscillation frequency. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: undamped simple harmonic motion obeys x = A cos(omega t), linking sinusoidal displacement, velocity, and acceleration curves via quarter-cycle phase shifts and gradients while kinetic and potential energy exchange at twice the oscillation frequency. Starting from x = +A at t = 0, displacement follows a cosine curve x = A cos(ωt). Velocity is the gradient of x–t, giving v = −v_max sin(ωt) with v_max = ωA, leading displacement by π/2 rad (a quarter period) so speed peaks at x = 0 (T/4 and 3T/4) and is zero at ±A. Acceleration is the gradient of v–t and obeys a = −ω²x, so a–t is an inverted cosine in antiphase (π rad) with x–t, peaking at ±ω²A at the extremes. Potential energy E_p = ½mω²x² peaks at 0, T/2, T while kinetic energy E_k peaks at T/4, 3T/4; both stay non-negative and oscillate at frequency 2f (period T/2) while E_k + E_p = E_tot stays constant.

Explain E_p and E_k oscillating at 2f (period T/2) between 0 and constant E_tot = ½mω²A².

items.stem: A 0.3 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness 25 N m⁻¹. It oscillates vertically with amplitude 0.024 m about equilibrium. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Δx_eq = mg / k = (0.3 × 9.8) / 25 = 0.118 m. (b) T = 2π√(0.3 / 25) = 0.688 s. (c) Maximum net SHM acceleration a_max = (k / m) x₀ = 2.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mg = k Δx_eq with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Evaluates a_max = ω² x₀ = (k / m) x₀.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes m = 0.4 kg, ω = 15 rad s⁻¹, and x₀ = 0.08 m into E_tot = ½mω²x₀².
Applies E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) or E_tot − ½mω²x².
Sets E_p = ½E_tot to obtain x = x₀ / √2.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total mechanical energy E_tot of the oscillating mass.
Calculate the kinetic energy E_k of the mass when its displacement is x = 0.04 m.
workingSteps: E_k = E_tot − E_p = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) = 0.216 J.

items.stem: A planetary refracting telescope operating in normal adjustment has an objective lens of focal length 2.10 m and produces an angular magnification of 60. Calculate the distance between the objective and eyepiece lenses.
items.workedSolution: From $M = \frac{f_o}{f_e}$, the eyepiece focal length is $f_e = \frac{2.10}{60} = 0.035\text{ m}$. In normal adjustment, the lens separation is $L = f_o + f_e = 2.10 + 0.035 = 2.14 m$.

items.stem: Narrow laser pulses enter a 1800 m step-index optical fibre from air (n_ext = 1.00, ray shown at 16.2°). The core refractive index is 1.49 and the cladding refractive index is 1.39. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) t_axial = n_core L / c = (1.49 × 1800) / 3.00 × 10⁸ = 8.94 × 10⁻⁶ s. (b) Longest guided ray has path L / sin θ_c = L n_core / n_clad, giving t_max = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 9.58 × 10⁻⁶ s. (c) Modal pulse delay Δt = t_max − t_axial = 6.43 × 10⁻⁷ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses t_axial = n_core L / c with n_core = 1.49 and L = 1800 m.
Applies L_max = L (n_core / n_clad) to find t_max = t_axial (n_core / n_clad).

items.stem: A steep light ray in water (n_ext = 1.33) enters a 350 m step-index optical fibre at 33.5° to the axis. The fibre has n_core = 1.52 and n_clad = 1.46, and light leaks into the cladding. At what angle to the wall normal does the ray refract in the cladding?
items.workedSolution: At entry, sin θ_axis = (1.33 sin 33.5°) / 1.52 ⇒ θ_axis = 28.9°. The angle to the wall normal is θ_w = 90° − θ_axis = 61.1° (< θ_c = 73.8°). Refracting into the cladding: sin θ_clad = (1.52 sin θ_w) / 1.46, giving θ_clad = 65.7°.

markScheme.criterion: Finds θ_w = 61.1° and refracts into cladding to obtain 65.7° (B).

items.stem: A narrow laser beam of vacuum wavelength 633 nm travels in water (n₁ = 1.33). It strikes a flat boundary with flint glass (n₂ = 1.65) at 26° to the normal. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Inside flint glass, v₂ = c / n₂ = 1.82 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and λ₂ = λ₀ / n₂ = 633 / 1.65 = 384 nm. (b) By Snell's law, sin θ₂ = (1.33 sin 26°) / 1.65, giving θ₂ = 20.7°. (c) Angular deviation δ = |θ₂ − θ₁| = 5.31°.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains λ₂ = 384 nm (with v₂ = 1.82 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹).
Substitutes n₁ = 1.33, θ₁ = 26°, and n₂ = 1.65 into n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

items.stem: A mass m = 0.4 kg hangs at rest from a vertical spring of stiffness k = 20 N m⁻¹. It is pulled down by x₀ = 0.032 m from equilibrium and released. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

items.stem: An undamped horizontal mass–spring oscillator completes one full simple harmonic oscillation every $T = 0.800\text{ s}$ with amplitude $x_0 = 12.0\text{ cm}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) simple harmonic motion requires a restoring acceleration directly proportional to displacement from equilibrium and always directed towards equilibrium. (b) the minus sign in a equals minus omega squared x shows that acceleration is always opposite to displacement and directed towards equilibrium. (c) $f = 1.25 Hz$ so $f_{E_k} = 2f = 2.50 Hz$. (d) kinetic energy is maximum at equilibrium and zero at amplitude extremes while potential energy peaks twice per cycle and total energy remains constant.

markScheme.criterion: States acceleration is proportional to displacement from equilibrium.

States restoring direction towards equilibrium (simple harmonic motion requires a restoring acceleration directly proportional to displacement from equilibrium and always directed towards equilibrium).
Notes acceleration vector always opposes displacement vector.

Links minus sign to restoring nature towards equilibrium (the minus sign in a equals minus omega squared x shows that acceleration is always opposite to displacement and directed towards equilibrium).
Finds oscillator frequency f = 1/T = 1.25 Hz and doubles for two equilibrium passes per cycle.
Identifies max E_k / zero E_p at x = 0 and max E_p / zero E_k at ±x₀.
States total energy remains constant (kinetic energy is maximum at equilibrium and zero at amplitude extremes while potential energy peaks twice per cycle and total energy remains constant).

items.stem: A student claims that hypermetropic reading spectacles work by making text look larger like a magnifying glass. Why is this statement physically misleading in A-Level Medical Physics?
items.workedSolution: Corrective spectacles work because the lens forms a virtual intermediate image at the unaided far or near point rather than magnifying the object, enabling the eye's lens to focus the rays onto the retina.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that forms a virtual intermediate image at the unaided far or near point rather than magnifying the object.

items.stem: A straight 60 m step-index optical fibre has n_core = 1.54 and n_clad = 1.45. Its flat entry face is in water (refractive index 1.33). A guided ray enters at θ_in = 12.4° to the axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) θ_c = arcsin(1.45 / 1.54) = 70.3°. (b) Using n_ext sin θ_max = √(n_core² − n_clad²) gives θ_max = 23.0°. (c) For θ_in = 12.4°, θ_axis = 10.7° and L_ray = 60 / cos θ_axis = 61.1 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies 1.33 sin θ_max = n_core sin(90° − θ_c).
Finds θ_axis = 10.7° and evaluates L / cos θ_axis.

items.stem: A 0.8 kg glider oscillates horizontally on a spring of stiffness 32 N m⁻¹. Its oscillation amplitude is 0.06 m. Find the frequency f in hertz.
items.workedSolution: Natural frequency f = (1 / 2π)√(k / m) = (1 / 2π)√(32 / 0.8) = 1.01 Hz.

options.label: D

items.workedSolution: (a) Snell's invariant n₀ sin θ₀ = 1.33 sin 32° = 0.705 (emergent angle = 32°). (b) Inside the slab, θ₁ = arcsin(0.7048 / 1.92) = 21.5°, so Δy = 0.06 tan θ₁ = 0.0237 m. (c) Perpendicular lateral displacement d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0117 m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds θ₁ = 21.5° and applies Δy = t₁ tan θ₁.
Applies d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ or (t₁ tan θ₀ − Δy) cos θ₀.

parts.prompt: State the emergent angle of refraction in water and calculate the optical Snell invariant n₀ sin θ₀.
workingSteps: Because both outer media have refractive index 1.33 and the faces are parallel, the emergent angle equals 32°.
Snell invariant = n₀ sin θ₀ = 1.33 × sin 32° = 0.705.

parts.prompt: Calculate the transverse offset Δy = t₁ tan θ₁ of the ray between the entry normal and exit normal along the slab face.
Hence calculate the perpendicular lateral displacement d between the emergent ray and the original incident ray line.
workingSteps: d = (t₁ tan θ₀ − Δy) cos θ₀ = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0117 m.

items.stem: A light ray travels inside zircon (n₁ = 1.92) towards a flat boundary with fused silica (n₂ = 1.46). It strikes the boundary at 58° to the normal. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) sin θ_c = 1.46 / 1.92, so θ_c = 49.5°. (b) Because n₁ > n₂ and θ₁ > θ_c, total internal reflection occurs at the interface. (c) Wave speed v₁ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.92 = 1.56 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and angular deviation δ = 180° − 2(58°) = 64.0°.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into sin θ_c = n₂ / n₁ = 1.46 / 1.92.
States total internal reflection because the ray is in the higher-index medium with incident angle greater than the critical angle.

items.stem: An electromagnetic shaker drives a trolley between two springs. The driving frequency is far higher than the trolley's natural frequency. What happens to the phase difference between the trolley and the shaker?
items.workedSolution: Well above f₀, inertia dominates and the oscillator moves in antiphase lagging the driving force by pi rad at high driving frequencies. Therefore the correct statement is: The trolley moves in antiphase lagging the driving force by pi rad at high driving frequencies

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: in antiphase lagging the driving force by pi rad at high driving frequencies.

options.label: A
options.text: The trolley moves completely in phase with the driving force with steadily rising amplitude.
options.distractorRationale: Ignores the inertia-dominated phase inversion above resonance.

options.label: B
options.text: The trolley moves in antiphase lagging the driving force by pi rad at high driving frequencies

options.label: C
options.text: The trolley moves with a fixed quarter-cycle lag at every frequency above the natural frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Assumes phase stops changing once resonance is crossed.

options.label: D
options.text: The trolley leads the driving force by half a cycle because spring stiffness exceeds inertia.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses lead/lag and confuses stiffness-dominated and inertia-dominated limits.

items.stem: What energy transformation explains why the peak displacement of a freely swinging pendulum in air gradually decreases over time?
items.workedSolution: Air drag acts opposite to velocity: a resistive damping force continuously transfers mechanical energy of the oscillator into thermal energy in the surroundings. Therefore the correct statement is: A resistive damping force continuously transfers mechanical energy of the oscillator into thermal energy in the surroundings

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: resistive damping force continuously transfers mechanical energy of the oscillator into thermal energy in the surroundings.

options.label: A
options.text: A restoring gravitational force gradually destroys mechanical energy as the amplitude shrinks.
options.distractorRationale: Violates conservation of energy; gravity is conservative and does not dissipate energy.

options.label: B
options.text: A centrifugal force converts kinetic energy into elastic potential energy in the string each half-cycle.
options.distractorRationale: Invokes a fictitious force and ignores air resistance dissipation.

options.label: C
options.text: A constant frictional force converts mechanical energy into gravitational potential energy stored in the air.
options.distractorRationale: Misidentifies the final energy store as gravitational potential energy rather than thermal energy.

options.label: D
options.text: A resistive damping force continuously transfers mechanical energy of the oscillator into thermal energy in the surroundings

items.stem: The graphs show resonance and phase-lag curves for a forced oscillator. Curves are plotted for light, moderate, and heavy viscous damping.
items.workedSolution: With greater damping, peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak broadens, and the peak frequency shifts slightly below the natural frequency. Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency f₀, giving maximum amplitude and the highest rate of energy transfer. As damping increases, more mechanical energy transfers to thermal energy each cycle, so amplitude drops at all frequencies, the peak broadens, and the peak shifts slightly below f₀. The displacement lags the driving force by about 0 rad when f << f₀ (in phase), by π/2 rad (90°) at f = f₀, and by about π rad (180°, antiphase) when f >> f₀.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States that resonance occurs when driving frequency equals the oscillator's natural frequency f₀, giving maximum amplitude.
L1b: Links resonance to the maximum rate of energy transfer from the periodic driver to the oscillator.
L2a: Explains that heavier damping lowers amplitude at all frequencies and broadens the resonance peak due to greater energy dissipation per cycle.
L2b: Explicitly notes that increasing damping shifts the resonant peak frequency slightly below f₀.
L3a: States that oscillator displacement lags driver by ~0 rad when f << f₀ and by π/2 rad (90°) at resonance f = f₀.
L3b: States that displacement lags driver by ~π rad (180°, antiphase) when f >> f₀, and notes heavier damping makes the phase transition more gradual.

parts.prompt: Explain the condition for resonance and describe how heavier damping changes the resonance curve. Explain how the phase lag between the oscillator and the driver changes from well below f₀ to well above f₀.
parts.expectedAnswer: With greater damping, peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak broadens, and the peak frequency shifts slightly below the natural frequency. Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency f₀, giving maximum amplitude and the highest rate of energy transfer. As damping increases, more mechanical energy transfers to thermal energy each cycle, so amplitude drops at all frequencies, the peak broadens, and the peak shifts slightly below f₀. The displacement lags the driving force by about 0 rad when f << f₀ (in phase), by π/2 rad (90°) at f = f₀, and by about π rad (180°, antiphase) when f >> f₀.
workingSteps: Define resonance via matching driving frequency to natural frequency f₀ and maximum energy transfer rate.
Detail all three effects of heavier damping: reduced amplitude everywhere, broader peak, and peak shifted slightly left of f₀.
Trace phase lag behind driver continuously from 0 (f << f₀) through π/2 rad at resonance (f = f₀) to π rad (f >> f₀).

items.stem: An engineer compares three damping designs for the pointer of an analogue balance. The designs use light air damping, electromagnetic critical damping, and heavy oil damping.
items.workedSolution: Critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating, while heavy damping returns more slowly. Light damping gives oscillations of nearly constant period inside an exponential decay envelope as mechanical energy transfers to thermal energy. Since total energy E is proportional to A², halving the amplitude leaves one quarter of the energy. Critical damping brings the pointer to its reading fastest without overshooting, whereas heavy overdamping creeps slowly back without oscillating. Critical damping is best for accurate instruments because the user avoids both decaying swings and slow settling.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Describes light damping as repeated oscillations with exponentially decreasing amplitude and approximately constant period.
L1b: States that dissipative forces convert mechanical energy into thermal energy and notes E ∝ A².
L2a: Defines critical damping accurately: returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating.
L2b: Describes heavy overdamping as non-oscillatory slow asymptotic approach taking longer than critical damping.
L3a: Selects critical damping as optimal for rapid accurate readings without pointer overshoot.
L3b: Contrasts operational drawbacks of light damping (waiting for swings to die down) and heavy damping (slow settling delay).

parts.prompt: Describe the displacement–time response of each damping regime when a test mass is placed on the pan. Explain why the fractional mechanical energy loss per cycle in light damping depends on amplitude squared. Evaluate which damping regime is best for rapid, accurate readings.

Light damping gives oscillations of nearly constant period inside an exponential decay envelope as mechanical energy transfers to thermal energy. Since total energy E is proportional to A², halving the amplitude leaves one quarter of the energy. Critical damping brings the pointer to its reading fastest without overshooting, whereas heavy overdamping creeps slowly back without oscillating. Critical damping is best for accurate instruments because the user avoids both decaying swings and slow settling.
workingSteps: Describe light, critical, and heavy damping responses clearly.
Relate light-damping energy decay to E ∝ A² and thermal dissipation.
Conclude why critical damping yields the fastest stable reading.

items.stem: A 1.2 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness 50 N m⁻¹. It then oscillates vertically with amplitude 0.024 m, where g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the static equilibrium extension Δx_eq of the spring?
items.workedSolution: At static equilibrium, upward spring tension balances weight: k Δx_eq = mg ⇒ Δx_eq = (1.2 × 9.8) / 50 = 0.235 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Hooke's law as k / (mg) instead of mg / k.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds the oscillation amplitude x₀ to mg / k, finding maximum total stretch rather than static equilibrium extension.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides mass m directly by spring constant k without multiplying by gravitational field strength g.

items.stem: A 0.5 kg mass oscillates in SHM with angular frequency ω = 12 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude x₀ = 0.12 m. What is its kinetic energy E_k at displacement x = 0.096 m?
items.workedSolution: Using E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) gives E_k = 0.5 × 0.5 × 12² × (0.12² − 0.096²) = 0.187 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the potential energy ½mω²x² at x rather than the kinetic energy ½mω²(x₀² − x²).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Interpolates energy linearly as E_tot(1 − x / x₀) instead of quadratically as E_tot(1 − x² / x₀²).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the total mechanical energy ½mω²x₀² instead of subtracting potential energy at x.

items.stem: Astronomers must choose between a large refracting telescope and a Cassegrain reflecting telescope of larger aperture. They want to observe very faint galaxies.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 response covers four areas. (1) Brightness and resolution: larger mirrors give collecting power proportional to diameter squared and smaller $\theta \approx \lambda / D$. (2) Aberrations: mirrors avoid chromatic aberration and a parabolic primary removes spherical aberration. (3) Construction: mirrors are back-supported and folded compactly, while heavy lenses sag and absorb light. (4) Trade-offs: the secondary mirror blocks some light and causes slight diffraction.

markScheme.criterion: States that mirrors can be built much larger than lenses because they are supported across the back rather than only at the edge.
Links larger aperture diameter to greater image brightness because collecting power is proportional to diameter squared.
Links larger aperture diameter to better angular resolution via the Rayleigh relation $\theta \approx \lambda / D$.
Explains that reflectors avoid chromatic aberration because reflection does not depend on wavelength, unlike glass refraction.
Explains that a parabolic primary mirror eliminates spherical aberration whereas thick lenses suffer glass absorption and sagging.
Evaluates reflector drawbacks accurately: secondary mirror and support struts block some light and cause additional diffraction.

parts.prompt: Compare the optical performance and construction of a refracting telescope and a Cassegrain reflecting telescope. Cover image brightness, resolving power, optical aberrations, and mechanical limits.
parts.expectedAnswer: A Cassegrain reflector outperforms a large refractor for faint deep-sky work because mirrors can be supported across their entire rear surface, enabling huge apertures with collecting power proportional to aperture diameter squared so far more photons are gathered per second and fainter galaxies become visible. Larger aperture diameter also improves angular resolution via $\theta \approx \lambda / D$. Unlike a glass refracting objective, reflection from the concave parabolic primary and convex secondary mirrors introduces zero chromatic aberration, and the parabolic curvature prevents on-axis spherical aberration. Large glass lenses can only be supported around their rim, causing sagging under gravity, glass absorption, bubbles, and very long heavy tubes. However, the Cassegrain secondary mirror and spider vanes obstruct a small fraction of incoming light and introduce slight diffraction spikes, and mirrors require periodic re-aluminising and collimation.
workingSteps: Link large mirror diameter to brighter images via collecting power proportional to diameter squared.
Link larger diameter to finer detail via Rayleigh criterion $\theta \approx \lambda / D$.
Contrast chromatic aberration in refractors with wavelength-independent reflection in Cassegrains.
Explain parabolic primary curvature eliminating on-axis spherical aberration.
Contrast rear-surface mirror support and compact folded path with rim-supported sagging lenses.
Note Cassegrain trade-offs: secondary mirror blockage, spider-vane diffraction, and alignment maintenance.

items.stem: An object performs SHM with frequency 8 Hz and amplitude 0.1 m. A reading is taken at x = 0.035 m. Find the size a_max of its maximum acceleration.
items.workedSolution: With ω = 2π(8) = 50.27 rad s⁻¹, maximum acceleration magnitude a_max = ω² x₀ = 253 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ω = 2πf and obtains 253 m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: A 1800 m step-index optical fibre has core index 1.49 and cladding index 1.39. Its end sits in air (n_ext = 1.00), with a 22.7° ray shown, and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Calculate the longest travel time for a guided ray along the fibre.
items.workedSolution: Wave speed in the core is v = c / n_core, and the critical-angle ray travels path length L / sin θ_c = L (n_core / n_clad). Therefore t_max = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 9.58 × 10⁻⁶ s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates t_max = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 9.58 × 10⁻⁶ s (A).

items.stem: A straight 120 m step-index optical fibre has a core (n_core = 1.52) and cladding (n_clad = 1.46). A narrow laser beam in air (n_ext = 1.00) meets the flat end at θ_in = 8.8° to the axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) sin θ_c = 1.46 / 1.52 ⇒ θ_c = 73.8°. (b) By Snell's law at the end-face, sin θ_axis = (1 sin 8.8°) / 1.52, so θ_axis = 5.78°. (c) Wall incident angle θ_w = 90° − θ_axis = 84.2°, which exceeds θ_c so the ray is guided by TIR.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts θ_axis from 90° to obtain θ_w.

items.stem: Light of vacuum wavelength 515 nm travels in air (refractive index 1). It meets a flat boundary with fused silica (refractive index 1.46) at 18° to the normal, with c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Calculate the angle of refraction in fused silica.
items.workedSolution: By Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, so sin θ₂ = (1 × sin 18°) / 1.46 = 0.2117. Taking the inverse sine gives θ₂ = 12.2°.

markScheme.criterion: Applies n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ to obtain θ₂ = 12.2° (A).

items.stem: A lit object of height 0.045 m is placed at u = 0.9 m in front of a thin concave lens (f = −0.3 m). Use the real-is-positive sign convention.
items.workedSolution: (a) Optical power P = 1 / (−0.3) = -3.33 D. (b) 1/v = −1/0.3 − 1/0.9 ⇒ v = -0.225 m. (c) Axial separation between object and virtual image on the same side = u − |v| = 0.675 m.

items.stem: A 0.2 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of constant 32 N m⁻¹. It oscillates vertically in SHM with amplitude 0.032 m, where g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the static equilibrium extension Δx_eq of the spring.
items.workedSolution: At static equilibrium, upward spring tension balances weight: k Δx_eq = mg ⇒ Δx_eq = (0.2 × 9.81) / 32 = 0.0613 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides mass m directly by spring constant k without multiplying by gravitational field strength g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds the oscillation amplitude x₀ to mg / k, finding maximum total stretch rather than static equilibrium extension.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Hooke's law as k / (mg) instead of mg / k.

items.stem: Simple harmonic motion is defined by the equation $a = -\omega^2 x$. What is the physical significance of the minus sign in this defining equation?
items.workedSolution: Because ω² > 0, the negative sign guarantees that a points towards x = 0 whenever x > 0 or x < 0, ensuring a restoring motion. Therefore the correct statement is: The minus sign in a equals minus omega squared x shows that acceleration is always opposite to displacement and directed towards equilibrium.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: the minus sign in a equals minus omega squared x shows that acceleration is always opposite to displacement and directed towards equilibrium.

items.stem: Opticians routinely correct myopia and hypermetropia using thin spectacle lenses placed just in front of the cornea.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 response: compares myopia (focus in front of retina, diverging $P < 0$) and hypermetropia (focus behind retina, converging $P > 0$). Clarifies that each lens forms a virtual intermediate image at the unaided far or near point rather than magnifying the object.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly states myopia is caused by an elongated eyeball or overly powerful cornea/lens focusing parallel rays in front of the retina.
Correctly explains myopia correction uses a diverging (negative power) lens creating a virtual image of distant objects at the unaided far point.
Correctly states hypermetropia is caused by a short eyeball or weak lens focusing near rays behind the retina.
Correctly explains hypermetropia correction uses a converging (positive power) lens creating a virtual image of a 0.25 m object at the unaided near point.
Clearly describes the ray path change before entering the cornea so the final real image lands sharply on the retina.
Explicitly refutes the magnification misconception by explaining spectacles reposition a virtual intermediate image into the eye's accommodation range.

parts.prompt: Compare the physical causes and ray paths of myopia and hypermetropia. Explain how each corrective spectacle lens works, and address the common misconception that spectacles simply magnify or shrink objects.
parts.expectedAnswer: In myopia (short sight), the eyeball is too long or the cornea and eye lens are too powerful, causing parallel rays from distant objects to converge and focus in front of the retina. A diverging (concave) spectacle lens with negative power diverges incoming parallel rays before they reach the eye so they appear to originate from a virtual image at the patient's unaided far point, allowing the relaxed eye to focus them sharply onto the retina. In hypermetropia (long sight), the eyeball is too short or the eye lens is too weak, so rays from a nearby object at $0.25\text{ m}$ would focus behind the retina. A converging (convex) spectacle lens with positive power reduces ray divergence so the lens forms a virtual intermediate image at the unaided far or near point rather than magnifying the object. Crucially, spectacles do not work by magnifying text; instead, they place an upright virtual image inside the patient's unaided range of accommodation so the eye can form a sharp real image on the retina.
workingSteps: Explain myopia anatomy: eyeball too long or cornea/lens too powerful; parallel rays focus in front of retina.
Explain myopia correction: negative-power diverging lens spreads parallel rays as if coming from unaided far point.
Explain hypermetropia anatomy: eyeball too short or lens too weak; near rays focus behind retina.
Explain hypermetropia correction: positive-power converging lens bends rays from 0.25 m to appear from unaided near point.
Clarify virtual upright intermediate image placement within the eye's natural range of accommodation.
Explicitly refute the misconception that spectacles work by magnifying the object.

items.workedSolution: Since sin θ_c = 1 / 1.65 gives θ_c = 37.3° and θ₁ = 50° > θ_c, total internal reflection occurs with θ_r = 50°. The angular deviation from the original forward direction is δ = 180° − 2(50°) = 80.0°.

items.stem: Inspecting the top (x–t) and bottom (a–t) traces for undamped simple harmonic motion, how does acceleration vary in phase relative to displacement?
items.workedSolution: Because a = −ω²x = −ω²A cos(ωt) = ω²A cos(ωt + π), acceleration and displacement are exactly π rad out of phase. Therefore the correct statement is: Directly from the defining SHM law, acceleration is always in antiphase with displacement with a phase difference of pi radians because acceleration equals minus omega squared times displacement.

items.stem: Total internal reflection (TIR) guides light along a step-index optical fibre. Which statement gives the exact two conditions needed at the core–cladding boundary?

options.label: A
options.text: Total internal reflection occurs when the core refractive index exceeds cladding index and angle of incidence is strictly greater than the critical angle

options.label: B
options.text: Total internal reflection occurs when the core refractive index exceeds cladding index and angle of incidence equals the critical angle
options.distractorRationale: At θ = θ_c, the ray refracts along the boundary (90°). TIR requires θ to be greater than θ_c.

options.label: C
options.text: Total internal reflection occurs when the cladding refractive index exceeds core index and angle of incidence is smaller than the critical angle
options.distractorRationale: Reverses both conditions; light must travel from optically denser core (n₁) toward less dense cladding (n₂).

options.label: D
options.text: Total internal reflection occurs when the fibre is bent sharply so the critical angle increases above ninety degrees
options.distractorRationale: AQA reject rule: bending a fibre changes the angle of incidence θ, NEVER the critical angle θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁).

items.stem: A moderately damped vibrator (f₀ = 6.4 Hz) is driven at its natural frequency with zero-frequency deflection A₀ = 14.0 mm and damping ratio ζ = 0.35. What is its steady-state amplitude A(f₀) = A₀ / (2ζ)?
items.workedSolution: Substituting into A(f₀) = A₀ / (2ζ) gives 14.0 / (2 × 0.35) = 20.0 mm.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes A₀ / ζ, dropping the factor of two.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the light damping ratio instead of moderate damping.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies static deflection by damping ratio.

items.stem: An analogue moving-coil galvanometer uses electromagnetic eddy-current damping on an aluminium former. Why is critical damping preferred over heavy damping for taking rapid scale readings?
items.workedSolution: Critical damping returns the pointer to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating. Heavy damping settles more slowly and delays readings, so option A is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: critical damping returns system to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating while heavy damping returns more slowly.

options.label: A
options.text: For rapid reading, critical damping returns system to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating while heavy damping returns more slowly

options.label: B
options.text: For rapid reading, heavy damping causes persistent sinusoidal swinging about the true current value.
options.distractorRationale: Attributes underdamped oscillation to heavy damping.

options.label: C
options.text: For rapid reading, critical damping amplifies the steady-state deflection angle of the pointer.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses damping with galvanometer sensitivity.

options.label: D
options.text: For rapid reading, heavy damping permanently locks the coil away from its equilibrium deflection.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses viscous or eddy-current damping (which drops to zero at zero angular speed) with static sticking.

items.stem: A load of mass m = 0.5 kg hangs at rest from a vertical spring (k = 25 N m⁻¹). It is pulled downwards by x₀ = 0.032 m and released. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Δx_eq = mg / k = (0.5 × 9.8) / 25 = 0.196 m. (b) T = 2π√(0.5 / 25) = 0.889 s. (c) Maximum net SHM acceleration a_max = (k / m) x₀ = 1.60 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mg = k Δx_eq with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Evaluates a_max = ω² x₀ = (k / m) x₀.

Determine the magnitude of the maximum net acceleration a_max of the mass during the oscillation.

items.stem: An undamped mass m = 0.6 kg moves in SHM with angular frequency ω = 25 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude x₀ = 0.04 m. Its energy is studied at displacement x = 0.02 m.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes m = 0.6 kg, ω = 25 rad s⁻¹, and x₀ = 0.04 m into E_tot = ½mω²x₀².
Applies E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) or E_tot − ½mω²x².
Sets E_p = ½E_tot to obtain x = x₀ / √2.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total mechanical energy E_tot of the oscillating mass.
Calculate the kinetic energy E_k of the mass when its displacement is x = 0.02 m.
workingSteps: E_k = E_tot − E_p = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) = 0.225 J.

parts.prompt: Determine the positive displacement x from equilibrium at which kinetic energy equals potential energy.

items.stem: A lit object of height h_o = 0.03 m stands at distance u = 0.252 m from a thin converging lens. The lens has focal length f = 0.18 m and forms a real, inverted image.
items.workedSolution: (a) 1/v = 1/0.18 − 1/0.252 ⇒ v = 0.630 m. (b) |m| = v / u = 2.50. (c) Object-to-screen separation = u + v = 0.882 m.

items.stem: An astronomical refracting telescope is set up in normal adjustment. Its objective focal length is 1.44 m, its eyepiece focal length is 0.024 m, and its aperture diameter is 0.12 m. What is the angular magnification of the telescope?
items.workedSolution: In normal adjustment, angular magnification is $M = \frac{f_o}{f_e} = \frac{1.44}{0.024} = 60.0$.

items.stem: A 1200 m step-index optical fibre has n_core = 1.5 and n_clad = 1.44. Its flat end sits in air (n_ext = 1.00), with a guided ray shown at 14.9°. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) t_axial = n_core L / c = (1.5 × 1200) / 3.00 × 10⁸ = 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ s. (b) Longest guided ray has path L / sin θ_c = L n_core / n_clad, giving t_max = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 6.25 × 10⁻⁶ s. (c) Modal pulse delay Δt = t_max − t_axial = 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses t_axial = n_core L / c with n_core = 1.5 and L = 1200 m.
Applies L_max = L (n_core / n_clad) to find t_max = t_axial (n_core / n_clad).

items.workedSolution: At the core–cladding boundary, sin θ_c = n_clad / n_core = 1.46 / 1.52 = 0.9605, giving θ_c = 73.8°.

items.stem: A narrow laser beam of vacuum wavelength 650 nm travels in flint glass (n₁ = 1.65). It strikes a flat boundary with fused silica (n₂ = 1.46) at 48° to the normal. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Inside fused silica, v₂ = c / n₂ = 2.05 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and λ₂ = λ₀ / n₂ = 650 / 1.46 = 445 nm. (b) By Snell's law, sin θ₂ = (1.65 sin 48°) / 1.46, giving θ₂ = 57.1°. (c) Angular deviation δ = |θ₂ − θ₁| = 9.12°.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains λ₂ = 445 nm (with v₂ = 2.05 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹).
Substitutes n₁ = 1.65, θ₁ = 48°, and n₂ = 1.46 into n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

items.stem: A single step-index glass fibre in a flexible gastroscope has a core refractive index $n_1 = 1.54$ and a cladding refractive index $n_2 = 1.44$. Calculate the critical angle $\theta_{\text{c}}$ at the core–cladding boundary.
items.workedSolution: Using $\sin\theta_{\text{c}} = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{1.44}{1.54} = 0.9351$, we obtain $\theta_{\text{c}} = \arcsin(0.9351) = 69.2 °$.

items.stem: An object of height 0.02 m sits 0.72 m from a thin diverging lens of focal length −0.4 m. Find the signed image position v in the real-is-positive convention.
items.workedSolution: For a diverging lens, f = −0.4 m. Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v gives 1/v = −1/0.4 − 1/0.72 = -3.889 m⁻¹, so v = -0.257 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses negative f = −0.4 m in 1/v = 1/f − 1/u to obtain v = -0.257 m (C).

items.stem: A 0.5 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness 25 N m⁻¹. It oscillates vertically with amplitude 0.055 m about equilibrium. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Δx_eq = mg / k = (0.5 × 9.81) / 25 = 0.196 m. (b) T = 2π√(0.5 / 25) = 0.889 s. (c) Maximum net SHM acceleration a_max = (k / m) x₀ = 2.75 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mg = k Δx_eq with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
Evaluates a_max = ω² x₀ = (k / m) x₀.

items.stem: The stacked graphs show the displacement $x$, velocity $v$, and acceleration $a$ of a particle in simple harmonic motion. Its amplitude is $x_0 = 10.0\text{ cm}$ and its period is $T = 1.60\text{ s}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\omega = 3.93 rad s⁻¹$. (b) $a_{\max} = 1.54 m s⁻²$. (c) velocity leads displacement by a quarter period while acceleration is half a period out of phase with displacement.

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_max = ω²x₀ with x₀ = 0.100 m.
States velocity leads displacement by T/4 (π/2 rad).
States acceleration is in antiphase with displacement (velocity leads displacement by a quarter period while acceleration is half a period out of phase with displacement).

items.stem: What details must an optician specify on a spectacle lens designed only to correct astigmatism?
items.workedSolution: Astigmatism requires a cylindrical lens specifying power and axis orientation so extra refractive power acts only along the misshapen meridian.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that cylindrical lens specifying power and axis orientation.

items.stem: A straight 300 m step-index optical fibre has core refractive index 1.52 and cladding refractive index 1.46. A laser ray in water (refractive index 1.33) enters the flat end at 8.3° to the axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) θ_c = arcsin(1.46 / 1.52) = 73.8°. (b) Using n_ext sin θ_max = √(n_core² − n_clad²) gives θ_max = 18.5°. (c) For θ_in = 8.3°, θ_axis = 7.26° and L_ray = 300 / cos θ_axis = 302 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies 1.33 sin θ_max = n_core sin(90° − θ_c).
Finds θ_axis = 7.26° and evaluates L / cos θ_axis.

items.stem: An upright object of height h_o = 0.018 m is placed at u = 0.084 m in front of a thin converging lens (f = 0.24 m). Use the real-is-positive convention (1/f = 1/u + 1/v, m = −v/u).

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes u = 0.084 m and f = 0.24 m into 1/v = 1/f − 1/u.

items.workedSolution: Using v = ω√(x₀² − x²) gives v = 30 × √(0.1² − 0.028²) = 2.88 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into v = ω√(x₀² − x²) to obtain 2.88 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: A 0.36 kg block oscillates horizontally on a spring with amplitude 0.09 m. Its measured period is 0.298 s. What is the spring constant k?
items.workedSolution: Rearranging T = 2π√(m / k) gives k = 4π²m / T² = 4π²(0.36) / (0.298)² = 160 N m⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts m / T² when rearranging the period equation.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 4π² and computes m / T².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Fails to square 2π / T when rearranging T = 2π√(m / k), computing 2πm / T instead of 4π²m / T².

items.stem: A narrow light beam travels in air (n₀ = 1). It enters a parallel-sided flint glass block (n₁ = 1.65, thickness 0.05 m) at 56° to the normal. The ray exits back into air on the far side.
items.workedSolution: (a) Snell's invariant n₀ sin θ₀ = 1 sin 56° = 0.829 (emergent angle = 56°). (b) Inside the slab, θ₁ = arcsin(0.8290 / 1.65) = 30.2°, so Δy = 0.05 tan θ₁ = 0.0291 m. (c) Perpendicular lateral displacement d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0252 m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds θ₁ = 30.2° and applies Δy = t₁ tan θ₁.
Applies d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ or (t₁ tan θ₀ − Δy) cos θ₀.

parts.prompt: State the emergent angle of refraction in air and calculate the optical Snell invariant n₀ sin θ₀.
workingSteps: Because both outer media have refractive index 1 and the faces are parallel, the emergent angle equals 56°.
Snell invariant = n₀ sin θ₀ = 1 × sin 56° = 0.829.

parts.prompt: Calculate the transverse offset Δy = t₁ tan θ₁ of the ray between the entry normal and exit normal along the slab face.
Hence calculate the perpendicular lateral displacement d between the emergent ray and the original incident ray line.
workingSteps: d = (t₁ tan θ₀ − Δy) cos θ₀ = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0252 m.

items.stem: A light ray travels inside flint glass (n₁ = 1.65) towards a flat boundary with air (n₂ = 1). It strikes the boundary at 50° to the normal. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) sin θ_c = 1 / 1.65, so θ_c = 37.3°. (b) Because n₁ > n₂ and θ₁ > θ_c, total internal reflection occurs at the interface. (c) Wave speed v₁ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.65 = 1.82 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and angular deviation δ = 180° − 2(50°) = 80.0°.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into sin θ_c = n₂ / n₁ = 1 / 1.65.
States total internal reflection because the ray is in the higher-index medium with incident angle greater than the critical angle.

State and explain the optical phenomenon that occurs when this beam meets the boundary.
parts.expectedAnswer: Total internal reflection occurs because light travels in the medium of higher refractive index and the incident angle exceeds the critical angle.
workingSteps: Compare incident angle with critical angle in the optically denser medium to confirm total internal reflection.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular deviation of the reflected ray from the incident ray's original forward direction, and find the wave speed in the first medium.
workingSteps: Wave speed in flint glass: v₁ = c / n₁ = 1.82 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
Angular deviation under total internal reflection: δ = 180° − 2(50°) = 80.0°.

items.stem: A 0.5 kg brass bob hangs on a 1.6 m light wire and swings with arc amplitude 0.448 m. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum tension in the wire at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: With ω = √(g / L) = √(9.81 / 1.6), peak speed v_max = ω x₀ = 1.11 m s⁻¹. At the lowest point, T_cord = m(g + v_max² / L) = 5.29 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_max = ω x₀ and T_cord = mg + mv_max² / L = 5.29 N (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the net radial centripetal force mv_max² / L rather than the total cord tension.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the centripetal force mv_max² / L from mg instead of adding it at the bottom of the arc.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates cord tension at the lowest point to static weight mg, ignoring the upward centripetal force mv_max² / L.

items.stem: A 0.40 kg glider on a smooth air track performs undamped SHM of amplitude A = 50 mm and period T = 1.00 s. It starts from x = +A at t = 0.
items.workedSolution: (a) 19.7 mJ. (b) 2.00 Hz. (c) kinetic energy and potential energy each oscillate between zero and the constant total energy twice per full cycle with period T/2 and frequency 2f.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = ½mω²A² with ω = 2π / 1.00 and A = 0.050 m.
Recognises kinetic energy peaks twice per period (f_E = 2f).
States E_k and E_p oscillate between 0 and E_tot with period T/2.
States E_k + E_p = E_tot remains horizontal and constant throughout.

items.stem: A $3.00\text{ km}$ medical-imaging optical fibre has core refractive index $1.50$ and cladding refractive index $1.44$. Take $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $v = 2.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $\theta_{\text{c}} = 73.7 °$. (b) Bending lowers $\theta$ (never $\theta_{\text{c}}$) causing partial refraction loss; modal dispersion arises from different ray path lengths whereas material dispersion arises from different wavelengths travelling at different speeds.

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): Bending decreases angle of incidence below θ_c while critical angle itself remains unchanged (reject 'critical angle changes').
L1 (Area 1): Some light refracts out into the cladding causing signal attenuation (reject 'all light escapes').
L2 (Area 2): Modal dispersion: rays entering at different angles follow different path lengths and arrive at different times.
L2 (Area 2): Modal dispersion reduced using a very narrow (single-mode) core.
L3 (Area 3): Material dispersion: different wavelengths travel at different speeds (different n); reduced with monochromatic light.
L3 (Area 3): Links both to pulse broadening, overlapping adjacent pulses, and reduced data transmission rate.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of light inside the core and the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary.
parts.expectedAnswer: Core speed $= 2.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹$; critical angle $= 73.7 °$

parts.prompt: Explain what happens if the fibre is bent too tightly so a ray strikes the boundary at $\theta < \theta_{\text{c}}$, and explain how modal dispersion and material dispersion degrade transmitted pulses and how engineers reduce both.
parts.expectedAnswer: Bending the fibre too tightly does not change the critical angle $\theta_{\text{c}}$, but reduces the angle of incidence below $\theta_{\text{c}}$ so some light refracts out into the cladding (attenuating the signal; do not say all light escapes). Alongside bend loss, modal dispersion arises from different ray path lengths whereas material dispersion arises from different wavelengths travelling at different speeds due to wavelength-dependent core refractive index. Both broaden output pulses until adjacent pulses overlap, limiting bandwidth; narrow single-mode cores mitigate modal dispersion while monochromatic laser light mitigates material dispersion.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Tight bend lowers angle of incidence below θ_c (θ_c unchanged) -> partial refraction out into cladding reduces intensity.
Area 2 (L2): Modal dispersion (path-length differences) + narrow core mitigation.
Area 3 (L3): Material dispersion (wavelength speed differences) + monochromatic laser mitigation + pulse overlap/data-rate link.

items.stem: Civil engineers add hydraulic fluid dampers to a pedestrian footbridge that previously swayed strongly under rhythmic footsteps. Which combination describes all three changes to the bridge's resonance curve?
items.workedSolution: Adding viscous dampers dissipates mechanical energy each cycle, so peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak broadens, and the peak frequency shifts slightly below the natural frequency. Therefore the correct statement is: Across the frequency spectrum, peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak broadens, and the peak frequency shifts slightly below the natural frequency

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak broadens, and the peak frequency shifts slightly below the natural frequency.

options.label: A
options.text: Across the frequency spectrum, peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak becomes sharper, and the peak frequency rises above the natural frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Incorrectly asserts a sharper peak and upward frequency shift with added damping.

options.label: B
options.text: Across the frequency spectrum, amplitude increases away from resonance while peak amplitude falls only at the exact natural frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Misinterprets curve broadening as an absolute amplitude increase off resonance.

options.label: C
options.text: Across the frequency spectrum, peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak broadens, and the peak frequency shifts slightly below the natural frequency

options.label: D
options.text: Across the frequency spectrum, the resonance curve shifts horizontally to higher frequencies with unchanged peak height.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses stiffening the structure with adding energy-dissipating damping.

items.stem: Why do vehicle suspension shock absorbers aim for approximately critical damping rather than heavy overdamping after hitting a road bump?
items.workedSolution: After a bump, critical damping returns system to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating while heavy damping returns more slowly. Therefore the correct statement is: Because critical damping returns system to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating while heavy damping returns more slowly

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: critical damping returns system to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating while heavy damping returns more slowly.

options.label: A
options.text: Because heavy damping causes the car body to bounce repeatedly for many cycles after each bump.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses underdamping/light damping with heavy damping.

options.label: B
options.text: Because critical damping eliminates all thermal dissipation in the shock absorber fluid.
options.distractorRationale: Forgets that critical damping still dissipates mechanical energy as heat.

options.label: C
options.text: Because critical damping returns system to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating while heavy damping returns more slowly

options.label: D
options.text: Because heavy damping lowers the car's natural frequency to zero so the tyres lift off the road immediately.
options.distractorRationale: Misstates the mechanism; heavy damping simply leaves the suspension slow to recover.

items.stem: A load of mass 1.2 kg hangs from a vertical spring of constant 100 N m⁻¹ and oscillates with amplitude 0.055 m. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the static extension Δx_eq at equilibrium?
items.workedSolution: At static equilibrium, upward spring tension balances weight: k Δx_eq = mg ⇒ Δx_eq = (1.2 × 9.8) / 100 = 0.118 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides mass m directly by spring constant k without multiplying by gravitational field strength g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds the oscillation amplitude x₀ to mg / k, finding maximum total stretch rather than static equilibrium extension.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Hooke's law as k / (mg) instead of mg / k.

items.stem: A 0.15 kg mass oscillates in SHM with ω = 15 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 0.12 m. A sensor monitors the mass at x = 0.06 m. Calculate the frequency f_E at which its kinetic energy oscillates.
items.workedSolution: Mechanical frequency f = ω / (2π) = 15 / (2π) = 2.387 Hz. Because kinetic energy reaches a maximum twice per mechanical period, f_E = 2f = ω / π = 4.77 Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates 2ω in rad s⁻¹ without dividing by 2π to convert to hertz.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Gives the mechanical displacement frequency f = ω / (2π) instead of recognizing that E_k ∝ cos²(ωt) oscillates at 2f.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Halves the mechanical frequency instead of doubling it.

markScheme.criterion: Finds v = 0.350 m and |m| = v / u = 1.33 (A).

items.stem: An object moves in SHM at frequency f = 12 Hz with amplitude x₀ = 0.08 m, as shown on the graph. Displacement to the right is positive. What is its signed acceleration a when x = 0.028 m?
items.workedSolution: Angular frequency ω = 2πf = 2π(12) = 75.40 rad s⁻¹. By the defining SHM equation, a = −ω²x = −(75.40)²(0.028) = -159 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ω = 2πf and obtains -159 m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: A short light pulse enters a 750 m step-index optical fibre (core index 1.6, cladding index 1.5). The end sits in air (n_ext = 1.00), with a 20.3° ray shown, and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Calculate the modal delay Δt = t_max − t_axial at the exit.
items.workedSolution: Axial transit time t_min = n_core L / c = (1.6 × 750) / (3.00 × 10⁸) = 4.00 × 10⁻⁶ s. At the critical angle sin θ_c = n_clad / n_core, t_max = t_min / sin θ_c = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 4.27 × 10⁻⁶ s. Modal delay Δt = t_max − t_min = 2.67 × 10⁻⁷ s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δt = (n_core L / c)(n_core / n_clad − 1) = 2.67 × 10⁻⁷ s (C).

items.stem: A 350 m step-index optical fibre has a glass core (n_core = 1.52) and cladding (n_clad = 1.46). Light enters from air (n_ext = 1.00) at 8.8° to the axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) sin θ_c = 1.46 / 1.52 ⇒ θ_c = 73.8°. (b) By Snell's law at the end-face, sin θ_axis = (1 sin 8.8°) / 1.52, so θ_axis = 5.78°. (c) Wall incident angle θ_w = 90° − θ_axis = 84.2°, which exceeds θ_c so the ray is guided by TIR.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts θ_axis from 90° to obtain θ_w.

Calculate the angle θ_axis that the refracted ray inside the core makes with the central axis.
workingSteps: n_ext sin θ_in = n_core sin θ_axis ⇒ sin θ_axis = (1 × sin 8.8°) / 1.52.

parts.prompt: Determine the angle of incidence θ_w of this ray on the core–cladding wall normal, confirming that total internal reflection occurs.

items.stem: A light ray in water (refractive index 1.33) meets a flat transparent sample at 48° to the normal. Inside the sample, the refracted ray travels at 36.8° to the normal. Find the refractive index n₂ of the sample.
items.workedSolution: Rearranging Snell's law n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ gives n₂ = 1.33 × sin 48° / sin 36.8° = 1.65.

items.stem: A flexible gastroscope contains two separate bundles of glass optical fibres ($n_1 = 1.55$, $n_2 = 1.43$) alongside an instrument channel for taking tissue biopsies.
items.workedSolution: (a) The coherent fibre bundle preserves spatial order of fibres to form an image; the non-coherent fibre bundle guides illumination light to internal tissue. (b) Each fibre acts as one pixel, so thinner fibres pack more pixels into the bundle cross-section and sharpen resolution. (c) $c_{\text{s}} = 3.00 \times 10^8 / 1.55 = 1.94 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Explains coherent fibre bundle preserves spatial order of fibres to form an image.
Explains non-coherent fibre bundle guides illumination light to internal tissue.
Notes each fibre carries a single image pixel.
Concludes thinner fibres allow more pixels per unit area, raising resolution.

Smaller diameter increases fibre count per unit area, improving spatial resolution.

items.stem: An object of height 0.036 m stands at u = 0.16 m from a thin concave lens of focal length f = −0.2 m. Use the real-is-positive sign convention throughout.
items.workedSolution: (a) Optical power P = 1 / (−0.2) = -5.00 D. (b) 1/v = −1/0.2 − 1/0.16 ⇒ v = -0.0889 m. (c) Axial separation between object and virtual image on the same side = u − |v| = 0.0711 m.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes f = −0.2 m and u = 0.16 m into 1/v = 1/f − 1/u.
Subtracts |v| from u because virtual image and object are on the same side of the lens.

items.stem: A 0.2 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness 100 N m⁻¹. It then oscillates vertically with amplitude 0.055 m, where g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the static equilibrium extension Δx_eq of the spring?
items.workedSolution: At static equilibrium, upward spring tension balances weight: k Δx_eq = mg ⇒ Δx_eq = (0.2 × 9.81) / 100 = 0.0196 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides mass m directly by spring constant k without multiplying by gravitational field strength g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds the oscillation amplitude x₀ to mg / k, finding maximum total stretch rather than static equilibrium extension.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Hooke's law as k / (mg) instead of mg / k.

items.stem: An optometrist records an astigmatic correction with cylindrical power -2.00 D oriented at an axis angle of 135°.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f = -0.500 m$. (b) cornea has different radii of curvature in perpendicular planes; cylindrical lens specifying power and axis orientation aligns power precisely with the defective meridian.

markScheme.criterion: States non-spherical cornea has different curvatures in perpendicular planes.
Identifies cylindrical lens acts along one plane only.

Explain why astigmatism occurs and why the prescription must include an axis orientation.
parts.expectedAnswer: Astigmatism occurs because the cornea has different radii of curvature in perpendicular planes; correcting it requires a cylindrical lens specifying power and axis orientation aligned with the misshapen corneal plane.
workingSteps: State unequal corneal curvature in perpendicular planes.
State cylindrical lens provides power in one meridian only.
Explain axis orientation aligns the lens power with the defective meridian.

items.stem: A 300 m step-index optical fibre has n_core = 1.54 and n_clad = 1.45. Light enters from air (refractive index 1.00), with a 22.5° ray shown. Find the largest angle of incidence θ_max to the axis for total internal reflection.
items.workedSolution: At the grazing limit, sin θ_c = 1.45 / 1.54, so inside the core sin θ_axis,max = cos θ_c = √(1 − (n_clad / n_core)²). By Snell's law at the entry face, n_ext sin θ_max = √(n_core² − n_clad²) = 0.5187, giving θ_max = arcsin(0.5187) = 31.2°.

markScheme.criterion: Uses n_ext sin θ_max = √(n_core² − n_clad²) to obtain θ_max = 31.2° (C).

items.stem: An object of height 0.015 m is placed 0.192 m in front of a convex magnifying lens of focal length 0.24 m. Calculate the height h_i of the upright virtual image.
items.workedSolution: From 1/v = 1/0.24 − 1/0.192, v = -0.960 m. Linear magnification m = −v / u = 5.000, so upright image height h_i = m h_o = 0.0750 m.

items.stem: A light ray passes from air (n₀ = 1) into a parallel-sided polycarbonate block (n₁ = 1.58, thickness 0.055 m). It enters at 34° to the normal and exits into fused silica (n₂ = 1.46). What is the angle of refraction in fused silica?
items.workedSolution: Across parallel flat boundaries, n₀ sin θ₀ = n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Thus sin θ₂ = (1 × sin 34°) / 1.46, giving θ₂ = 22.5°.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Snell invariant n₀ sin θ₀ = n₂ sin θ₂ to obtain θ₂ = 22.5° (C).

items.stem: Light travels from a transparent block towards a flat boundary with fused silica (n₂ = 1.46). The critical angle for total internal reflection is 37.1° to the normal. What is the refractive index n₁ of the block?
items.workedSolution: At the critical angle, n₁ sin θ_c = n₂ sin 90° = n₂, so n₁ = 1.46 / sin 37.1° = 2.42.

markScheme.criterion: Computes n₁ = n₂ / sin θ_c = 1.46 / sin 37.1° = 2.42 (D).
