items.stem: A pendulum bob of mass m = 0.6 kg hangs from a light string of length L = 1.9 m. It swings in small-angle SHM with arc amplitude x₀ = 0.532 m. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) T = 2π√(1.9 / 9.81) = 2.77 s. (b) v_max = √(9.81 / 1.9) × 0.532 = 1.21 m s⁻¹. (c) Lowest-point cord tension = m(g + v_max² / L) = 6.35 N.

markScheme.criterion: Applies v_max = ω x₀ = (2π / T) x₀.
Uses T_cord = mg + mv_max² / L at the bottom of the arc.

parts.prompt: Calculate the period T of the pendulum.
Calculate the maximum speed v_max of the bob as it passes through equilibrium.
Determine the tension in the suspension cord as the bob passes through its lowest point.

items.stem: How are the shapes of the x–t, v–t, and a–t graphs mathematically connected across each quarter-period T/4?
items.workedSolution: Steepest negative slope on x–t at t = T/4 matches the negative trough of v–t; zero slope on v–t at t = T/4 matches a = 0. Therefore the correct statement is: At every instant during the oscillation, velocity at any instant equals the gradient of the displacement-time graph and acceleration equals the gradient of the velocity-time graph.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: velocity at any instant equals the gradient of the displacement-time graph and acceleration equals the gradient of the velocity-time graph.

options.label: A
options.text: Displacement equals the gradient of the velocity-time graph and velocity equals the gradient of the acceleration-time graph.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the derivative/area relationship: area under v–t gives Δx, whereas gradient of x–t gives v.

options.label: B
options.text: At every instant during the oscillation, velocity at any instant equals the gradient of the displacement-time graph and acceleration equals the gradient of the velocity-time graph.

options.label: C
options.text: Acceleration equals the gradient of the displacement-time graph whenever the oscillator crosses equilibrium.
options.distractorRationale: The gradient of x–t is velocity v (maximum at x = 0), where acceleration is zero.

options.label: D
options.text: All three graphs have zero gradient at the same instants t = 0, T/2, and T.
options.distractorRationale: At t = 0, x–t and a–t have zero gradient, while v–t has its steepest negative gradient (−a_max).

items.stem: A $1.50\text{ km}$ step-index optical fibre has $n_1 = 1.52$ and $n_2 = 1.46$. Using $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, calculate the maximum modal arrival-time difference (in nanoseconds) between an axial ray and a ray reflecting at the critical angle.
items.workedSolution: Core speed $v = c/n_1 = 1.974 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$; axial time $t_{\min} = L/v = 7.60 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}$; longest guided path $L/\sin\theta_{\text{c}} = L(n_1/n_2)$, so $\Delta t = t_{\min}(n_1/n_2 - 1) = 312 ns$. Option C (312 ns) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Modal delay $= 312 ns$ (312 ns, option C).

items.stem: A bridge deck model is vibrated by a motor operating at a driving frequency far below the model's natural frequency. How does the bridge displacement behave relative to the driver?
items.workedSolution: At very slow driving speeds inertia is negligible, so the oscillator follows the driver in phase with the driving force at frequencies well below the natural frequency. Therefore the correct statement is: It oscillates almost in phase with the driving force at frequencies well below the natural frequency

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: in phase with the driving force at frequencies well below the natural frequency.

options.label: A
options.text: It oscillates almost in phase with the driving force at frequencies well below the natural frequency

options.label: B
options.text: It oscillates almost in antiphase with the driving force at frequencies well below the natural frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the low-frequency and high-frequency phase regimes.

options.label: C
options.text: It lags the driving force by a quarter cycle at all frequencies below the natural frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Incorrectly treats the resonance phase lag as constant throughout the sub-resonant range.

options.label: D
options.text: It oscillates only at its natural frequency while ignoring the slow driver completely.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses initial free oscillation with steady-state forced oscillation.

items.stem: A metal bob hangs from a spring and oscillates freely in air. Each peak amplitude drops by a constant fraction every cycle. How is this motion best described?
items.workedSolution: Light damping causes an exponentially decaying oscillation with approximately constant period. Therefore the correct statement is: Light damping produces an exponentially decaying oscillation with approximately constant period

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: exponentially decaying oscillation with approximately constant period.

options.label: A
options.text: Light damping produces a linear decrease in amplitude to zero while the period halves every cycle.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses exponential decay with linear decay and wrongly assumes period halves.

options.label: B
options.text: Light damping produces an immediate return to equilibrium without crossing the centre line.
options.distractorRationale: Describes critical or heavy damping rather than light damping.

options.label: C
options.text: Light damping produces constant amplitude with steadily decreasing frequency until motion stops.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses what decays in light viscous damping.

options.label: D
options.text: Light damping produces an exponentially decaying oscillation with approximately constant period

items.stem: A 0.75 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness 40 N m⁻¹. It oscillates vertically with amplitude 0.055 m about equilibrium. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Δx_eq = mg / k = (0.75 × 9.8) / 40 = 0.184 m. (b) T = 2π√(0.75 / 40) = 0.860 s. (c) Maximum net SHM acceleration a_max = (k / m) x₀ = 2.93 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mg = k Δx_eq with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Evaluates a_max = ω² x₀ = (k / m) x₀.

items.stem: A mass m = 1.2 kg oscillates in undamped SHM with ω = 25 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude x₀ = 0.1 m. The energy–displacement graph is read at displacement x = 0.05 m.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes m = 1.2 kg, ω = 25 rad s⁻¹, and x₀ = 0.1 m into E_tot = ½mω²x₀².
Applies E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) or E_tot − ½mω²x².
Sets E_p = ½E_tot to obtain x = x₀ / √2.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total mechanical energy E_tot of the oscillating mass.
Calculate the kinetic energy E_k of the mass when its displacement is x = 0.05 m.
workingSteps: E_k = E_tot − E_p = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) = 2.81 J.

items.stem: On an optical bench, a bright object of height 0.036 m sits 1 m from a thin convex lens (focal length 0.25 m). A real image forms on a screen.
items.workedSolution: (a) 1/v = 1/0.25 − 1/1 ⇒ v = 0.333 m. (b) |m| = v / u = 0.333. (c) Object-to-screen separation = u + v = 1.33 m.

items.stem: A single crown-glass objective lens in a refractor suffers from chromatic aberration. It focuses blue light at 1.624 m and red light at 1.662 m along the principal axis. What is the axial distance between the blue and red focal points?
items.workedSolution: Blue light has a larger refractive index in glass and bends more strongly ($f_{\text{blue}} < f_{\text{red}}$). The axial focal spread is $\Delta f = 1.662 - 1.624 = 0.038\text{ m} = 38.0 mm$.

items.stem: Narrow laser pulses enter a 150 m step-index optical fibre from air (n_ext = 1.00, ray shown at 15.9°). The core refractive index is 1.58 and the cladding refractive index is 1.49. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) t_axial = n_core L / c = (1.58 × 150) / 3.00 × 10⁸ = 7.90 × 10⁻⁷ s. (b) Longest guided ray has path L / sin θ_c = L n_core / n_clad, giving t_max = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 8.38 × 10⁻⁷ s. (c) Modal pulse delay Δt = t_max − t_axial = 4.77 × 10⁻⁸ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses t_axial = n_core L / c with n_core = 1.58 and L = 150 m.
Applies L_max = L (n_core / n_clad) to find t_max = t_axial (n_core / n_clad).

items.stem: Light in water (n_ext = 1.33) enters a 120 m step-index optical fibre at 15.6° to the axis. The fibre has n_core = 1.58 and n_clad = 1.49. Find the angle of incidence θ_w at the core–cladding boundary, measured to the normal.
items.workedSolution: At the entry face, 1.33 sin 15.6° = 1.58 sin θ_axis ⇒ θ_axis = 13.1°. Since the core wall is parallel to the axis, its normal is perpendicular to the axis, giving θ_w = 90° − θ_axis = 76.9°.

items.stem: A narrow light ray of vacuum wavelength 488 nm travels through water (n₁ = 1.33). It meets a smooth sapphire surface (n₂ = 1.77) at 26° to the normal. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Inside sapphire, v₂ = c / n₂ = 1.69 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and λ₂ = λ₀ / n₂ = 488 / 1.77 = 276 nm. (b) By Snell's law, sin θ₂ = (1.33 sin 26°) / 1.77, giving θ₂ = 19.2°. (c) Angular deviation δ = |θ₂ − θ₁| = 6.77°.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains λ₂ = 276 nm (with v₂ = 1.69 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹).
Substitutes n₁ = 1.33, θ₁ = 26°, and n₂ = 1.77 into n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

items.stem: A step-index imaging fibre ($n_1 = 1.58$, $n_2 = 1.45$) receives light from air ($n = 1.00$) at its flat end. What is the largest angle of incidence in air for which total internal reflection still occurs at the core–cladding boundary?
items.workedSolution: At the critical boundary $\sin\theta_{\text{c}} = \frac{1.45}{1.58}$, so the internal angle to the axis is $90^\circ - \theta_{\text{c}}$. Applying Snell's law at the end face gives $\sin\theta_{\text{a}} = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2} = 0.628$, hence $\theta_{\text{a}} = 38.9 °$.

items.stem: An upright object of height 0.036 m sits at u = 1 m in front of a thin diverging lens (f = −0.4 m). What is the linear magnification m = −v / u of the virtual image?

items.stem: A mass m = 0.75 kg hangs at rest from a vertical spring of stiffness k = 25 N m⁻¹. It is pulled down by x₀ = 0.024 m from equilibrium and released. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Δx_eq = mg / k = (0.75 × 9.81) / 25 = 0.294 m. (b) T = 2π√(0.75 / 25) = 1.09 s. (c) Maximum net SHM acceleration a_max = (k / m) x₀ = 0.800 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mg = k Δx_eq with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
Evaluates a_max = ω² x₀ = (k / m) x₀.

items.stem: A myopic student has an unaided far point of 0.500 m and an unaided near point of 0.125 m. While wearing spectacles prescribed to correct distant vision, what is the student's new closest clear-viewing distance?
items.workedSolution: The spectacles have power $P = -\frac{1}{0.500} = -2.00\text{ D}$. For a virtual image at the eye's unaided near point ($v = -0.125\text{ m}$), $\frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{v} = -2.00 - (-8.00) = 6.00\text{ m}^{-1}$, giving $u = 0.167 m$.

items.stem: A straight 750 m step-index optical fibre has a core (n_core = 1.62) and cladding (n_clad = 1.51). Its flat end sits in air of refractive index 1.00. A light ray enters at θ_in = 25.9° to the axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) θ_c = arcsin(1.51 / 1.62) = 68.8°. (b) Using n_ext sin θ_max = √(n_core² − n_clad²) gives θ_max = 35.9°. (c) For θ_in = 25.9°, θ_axis = 15.6° and L_ray = 750 / cos θ_axis = 779 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies 1 sin θ_max = n_core sin(90° − θ_c).
Finds θ_axis = 15.6° and evaluates L / cos θ_axis.

items.stem: An upright object of height h_o = 0.008 m is placed at u = 0.032 m in front of a thin converging lens (f = 0.08 m). Use the real-is-positive convention (1/f = 1/u + 1/v, m = −v/u).
items.workedSolution: (a) 1/v = 1/0.08 − 1/0.032 ⇒ v = -0.0533 m (virtual, since v < 0). (b) m = −v / u = 1.67. (c) Upright virtual image height h_i = m h_o = 0.0133 m.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes u = 0.032 m and f = 0.08 m into 1/v = 1/f − 1/u.
Multiplies magnification m by object height h_o.

items.stem: An object oscillates in SHM with amplitude 0.1 m and angular frequency 20 rad s⁻¹. Find its speed |v| = ω√(x₀² − x²) at displacement x = 0.028 m.
items.workedSolution: Using v = ω√(x₀² − x²) gives v = 20 × √(0.1² − 0.028²) = 1.92 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into v = ω√(x₀² − x²) to obtain 1.92 m s⁻¹ (C).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates ω(x₀ − x) linearly instead of taking √(x₀² − x²).

items.stem: A 0.25 kg block oscillates horizontally on a spring with amplitude 0.025 m. Its measured period is 0.740 s. What is the spring constant k?
items.workedSolution: Rearranging T = 2π√(m / k) gives k = 4π²m / T² = 4π²(0.25) / (0.740)² = 18.0 N m⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 4π² and computes m / T².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Fails to square 2π / T when rearranging T = 2π√(m / k), computing 2πm / T instead of 4π²m / T².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts m / T² when rearranging the period equation.

items.stem: A narrow light beam travels in air (n₀ = 1). It enters a parallel-sided crown glass block (n₁ = 1.52, thickness 0.075 m) at 44° to the normal. The ray exits back into air on the far side.
items.workedSolution: (a) Snell's invariant n₀ sin θ₀ = 1 sin 44° = 0.695 (emergent angle = 44°). (b) Inside the slab, θ₁ = arcsin(0.6947 / 1.52) = 27.2°, so Δy = 0.075 tan θ₁ = 0.0385 m. (c) Perpendicular lateral displacement d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0244 m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds θ₁ = 27.2° and applies Δy = t₁ tan θ₁.
Applies d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ or (t₁ tan θ₀ − Δy) cos θ₀.

parts.prompt: State the emergent angle of refraction in air and calculate the optical Snell invariant n₀ sin θ₀.
workingSteps: Because both outer media have refractive index 1 and the faces are parallel, the emergent angle equals 44°.
Snell invariant = n₀ sin θ₀ = 1 × sin 44° = 0.695.

parts.prompt: Calculate the transverse offset Δy = t₁ tan θ₁ of the ray between the entry normal and exit normal along the slab face.
Hence calculate the perpendicular lateral displacement d between the emergent ray and the original incident ray line.
workingSteps: d = (t₁ tan θ₀ − Δy) cos θ₀ = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0244 m.

items.stem: A light ray travels inside zircon (n₁ = 1.92) towards a flat boundary with air (n₂ = 1). It strikes the boundary at 44° to the normal. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) sin θ_c = 1 / 1.92, so θ_c = 31.4°. (b) Because n₁ > n₂ and θ₁ > θ_c, total internal reflection occurs at the interface. (c) Wave speed v₁ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.92 = 1.56 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and angular deviation δ = 180° − 2(44°) = 92.0°.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into sin θ_c = n₂ / n₁ = 1 / 1.92.
States total internal reflection because the ray is in the higher-index medium with incident angle greater than the critical angle.

parts.prompt: Calculate the critical angle θ_c at the zircon–air boundary.
State and explain the optical phenomenon that occurs when this beam meets the boundary.
parts.expectedAnswer: Total internal reflection occurs because light travels in the medium of higher refractive index and the incident angle exceeds the critical angle.
workingSteps: Compare incident angle with critical angle in the optically denser medium to confirm total internal reflection.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular deviation of the reflected ray from the incident ray's original forward direction, and find the wave speed in the first medium.
workingSteps: Wave speed in zircon: v₁ = c / n₁ = 1.56 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
Angular deviation under total internal reflection: δ = 180° − 2(44°) = 92.0°.

items.stem: A 0.5 kg brass bob hangs on a 0.72 m light wire and swings with arc amplitude 0.18 m. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the maximum tension in the wire at the lowest point.
items.workedSolution: With ω = √(g / L) = √(9.81 / 0.72), peak speed v_max = ω x₀ = 0.664 m s⁻¹. At the lowest point, T_cord = m(g + v_max² / L) = 5.21 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_max = ω x₀ and T_cord = mg + mv_max² / L = 5.21 N (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the net radial centripetal force mv_max² / L rather than the total cord tension.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the centripetal force mv_max² / L from mg instead of adding it at the bottom of the arc.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Equates cord tension at the lowest point to static weight mg, ignoring the upward centripetal force mv_max² / L.

items.stem: An undamped oscillator has oscillation period T = 0.64 s. What is the frequency with which its kinetic energy E_k oscillates between zero and E_tot?
items.workedSolution: Displacement frequency f = 1 / 0.64 = 1.56 Hz; kinetic energy reaches maximum twice per oscillation, so f_E = 2f = 3.13 Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Determines kinetic energy oscillation frequency = 3.13 Hz.

items.stem: Step-index optical fibres carry high-speed digital data using pulses of light. The light travels along a glass core surrounded by glass cladding, as shown.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 (5–6 marks): Explains core and cladding roles and $\theta > \theta_{\text{c}}$ for TIR. Distinguishes modal dispersion (different ray path lengths) from material dispersion (different wavelengths moving at different speeds; max L2 if swapped). Gives both fixes (narrow core; monochromatic light) and links them to pulse overlap and lower data rate.

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): Core has higher refractive index than cladding (n₁ > n₂) and guides light by TIR when angle of incidence is greater than critical angle (reject 'at critical angle').
L1 (Area 1): Cladding protects core surface from scratches, prevents crosstalk between touching fibres, and provides clean lower-index TIR boundary.
L2 (Area 2): Modal dispersion: rays enter at different angles and follow different path lengths, arriving at different times.
L2 (Area 2): Modal dispersion reduced by using a very narrow core (single-mode fibre) or smaller core–cladding index difference.

L3 (Area 3): Material dispersion: different wavelengths travel at different speeds because refractive index varies with wavelength; reduced using monochromatic light (max L2 if modal & material swapped).
L3 (Area 3): Links both dispersion mechanisms to pulse broadening, overlapping pulses, signal corruption, and reduced maximum data rate.

parts.prompt: Explain the role of the core and cladding in an optical fibre. Distinguish between modal dispersion and material dispersion, and explain their effect on digital signals. State how each type of dispersion is reduced.
parts.expectedAnswer: The low-absorption core ($n_1 > n_2$) guides pulses by total internal reflection whenever the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle ($\theta > \theta_{\text{c}}$, not equal to it). The lower-index cladding protects the core from scratches, prevents crosstalk between fibres, and gives a clean boundary for TIR. Modal dispersion arises from different ray path lengths, whereas material dispersion arises from different wavelengths travelling at different speeds because refractive index depends on wavelength. Both cause pulse broadening, so pulses overlap, corrupt data, and lower the maximum data rate. Modal dispersion is reduced with a very narrow (single-mode) core (or small $n_1 - n_2$), while material dispersion is reduced using monochromatic laser light.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Core (n₁ > n₂, TIR for θ > θ_c only) and cladding (scratch protection, no crosstalk, TIR boundary).
Area 2 (L2): Modal dispersion = different entry angles/path lengths -> mitigated by narrow core.
Area 3 (L3): Material dispersion = different wavelengths travel at different speeds (n varies with λ) -> mitigated by monochromatic light; link both to pulse broadening/overlap/data rate limit.

items.stem: An acoustic resonator with natural frequency f₀ = 10.0 Hz experiences moderate viscous damping with ζ = 0.40. Using f_peak = f₀ √(1 − 2ζ²), determine the shifted frequency at which its driven amplitude reaches a maximum.

markScheme.criterion: Finds shifted resonant peak frequency 8.25 Hz.

options.distractorRationale: Uses √(1 − ζ²) instead of √(1 − 2ζ²).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to take the square root.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Shifts the resonant peak upward above f₀ instead of downward.

items.stem: The amplitude of a lightly damped harmonic oscillator decreases to 0.80 of its previous value on each complete cycle. What percentage of the oscillator's mechanical energy is dissipated during one cycle?
items.workedSolution: Total mechanical energy E ∝ A², so remaining fraction is 0.80² = 0.64. Percentage lost = (1 − 0.64) × 100% = 36.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses E ∝ A² to find 36.0% energy lost per cycle.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes energy is proportional to amplitude A rather than A².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reports the percentage of energy remaining (0.80² = 64%) rather than energy lost.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Reports the amplitude retention ratio directly as a percentage.

items.stem: A 0.2 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring (k = 32 N m⁻¹) where g = 9.8 m s⁻². It oscillates vertically with amplitude 0.032 m. Find the period T of the oscillation.
items.workedSolution: Gravity shifts the equilibrium position without altering effective stiffness k, so T = 2π√(m / k) = 2π√(0.2 / 32) = 0.497 s.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes the oscillation amplitude x₀ into a pendulum-style formula 2π√(x₀ / g) instead of 2π√(m / k).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Incorrectly adds weight mg to spring stiffness k, assuming gravity changes the vertical mass-spring period.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Swaps m/k and k/m inside the square root.

items.stem: A 0.25 kg mass oscillates in SHM with ω = 18 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 0.06 m. A sensor monitors the mass at x = 0.015 m. Calculate the frequency f_E at which its kinetic energy oscillates.
items.workedSolution: Mechanical frequency f = ω / (2π) = 18 / (2π) = 2.865 Hz. Because kinetic energy reaches a maximum twice per mechanical period, f_E = 2f = ω / π = 5.73 Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates 2ω in rad s⁻¹ without dividing by 2π to convert to hertz.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Gives the mechanical displacement frequency f = ω / (2π) instead of recognizing that E_k ∝ cos²(ωt) oscillates at 2f.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Halves the mechanical frequency instead of doubling it.

items.stem: An object of height 0.036 m sits at u = 0.8 m in front of a thin convex lens of focal length 0.25 m. A sharp real image forms on a screen. Calculate the linear magnification |m| of the image.

markScheme.criterion: Finds v = 0.364 m and |m| = v / u = 0.455 (B).

items.stem: A research Cassegrain telescope has a 4.00 m diameter primary mirror with an effective focal length of 18.0 m. When fitted with a visual eyepiece in normal adjustment, its angular magnification is 400.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_e = 18.0 / 400 = 0.0450 m$. (b) $f_o / D = 18.0 / 4.00 = 4.50$. (c) Uses a concave parabolic primary mirror and convex secondary mirror, eliminating spherical aberration for on-axis parallel rays.

markScheme.criterion: Divides effective focal length by aperture diameter.
States concave parabolic primary and convex secondary mirrors.
Explains parabolic curvature focuses outer and inner parallel rays to one point.

items.stem: An object moves in SHM at frequency f = 6 Hz with amplitude x₀ = 0.02 m, as shown on the graph. Displacement to the right is positive. What is its signed acceleration a when x = 0.007 m?
items.workedSolution: Angular frequency ω = 2πf = 2π(6) = 37.70 rad s⁻¹. By the defining SHM equation, a = −ω²x = −(37.70)²(0.007) = -9.95 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ω = 2πf and obtains -9.95 m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: A 240 m step-index optical fibre has n_core = 1.57 and n_clad = 1.46, in air (n_ext = 1.00). A guided ray is shown entering at 17.6°, and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Find the modal dispersion delay Δt between the slowest guided ray and the axial ray.
items.workedSolution: Axial transit time t_min = n_core L / c = (1.57 × 240) / (3.00 × 10⁸) = 1.26 × 10⁻⁶ s. At the critical angle sin θ_c = n_clad / n_core, t_max = t_min / sin θ_c = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 1.35 × 10⁻⁶ s. Modal delay Δt = t_max − t_min = 9.46 × 10⁻⁸ s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δt = (n_core L / c)(n_core / n_clad − 1) = 9.46 × 10⁻⁸ s (C).

items.stem: An 80 m step-index optical fibre consists of a glass core (n_core = 1.6) inside cladding (n_clad = 1.5). A light ray in air (n_ext = 1.00) enters the flat end at 17.3° to the axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) sin θ_c = 1.5 / 1.6 ⇒ θ_c = 69.6°. (b) By Snell's law at the end-face, sin θ_axis = (1 sin 17.3°) / 1.6, so θ_axis = 10.7°. (c) Wall incident angle θ_w = 90° − θ_axis = 79.3°, which exceeds θ_c so the ray is guided by TIR.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts θ_axis from 90° to obtain θ_w.

items.stem: A light beam of vacuum wavelength 670 nm meets a flat ethanol–zircon boundary (n₁ = 1.36, n₂ = 1.92). Its angle of incidence is 42° to the normal, and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Find the speed of the refracted wave in zircon.
items.workedSolution: From the definition of refractive index n₂ = c / v₂, the wave speed in zircon is v₂ = (3.00 × 10⁸) / 1.92 = 1.56 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes v₂ = c / n₂ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.92 = 1.56 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: A lit object of height 0.045 m is placed at u = 0.72 m in front of a thin concave lens (f = −0.4 m). Use the real-is-positive sign convention.
items.workedSolution: (a) Optical power P = 1 / (−0.4) = -2.50 D. (b) 1/v = −1/0.4 − 1/0.72 ⇒ v = -0.257 m. (c) Axial separation between object and virtual image on the same side = u − |v| = 0.463 m.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes f = −0.4 m and u = 0.72 m into 1/v = 1/f − 1/u.
Subtracts |v| from u because virtual image and object are on the same side of the lens.

Calculate the signed image distance v using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.
Determine the axial distance between the object and its virtual image.
workingSteps: Both lie on the input side of the lens, so separation = u − |v| = |u + v| = 0.463 m.

items.stem: A 0.75 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring (k = 100 N m⁻¹) where g = 9.81 m s⁻². It oscillates vertically with amplitude 0.032 m. Find the period T of the oscillation.
items.workedSolution: Gravity shifts the equilibrium position without altering effective stiffness k, so T = 2π√(m / k) = 2π√(0.75 / 100) = 0.544 s.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Incorrectly adds weight mg to spring stiffness k, assuming gravity changes the vertical mass-spring period.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes the oscillation amplitude x₀ into a pendulum-style formula 2π√(x₀ / g) instead of 2π√(m / k).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Swaps m/k and k/m inside the square root.

items.stem: In HL simple harmonic motion, displacement is modelled by $x = x_0 \sin(\omega t + \phi)$ where $\phi$ is measured in radians. Compared with $x = x_0 \sin(\omega t)$, what is the effect of introducing a positive phase angle $0 < \phi < \pi/2$?
items.workedSolution: At t = 0, x(0) = x₀ sin ϕ > 0 and v(0) = ωx₀ cos ϕ > 0; adding positive ϕ shifts the sine curve leftward (earlier in time). Therefore the correct statement is: A positive phase angle phi in radians shifts the sinusoidal oscillation earlier in time so displacement is non-zero at t equals zero.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: a positive phase angle phi in radians shifts the sinusoidal oscillation earlier in time so displacement is non-zero at t equals zero.

options.text: A positive phase angle phi in radians shifts the sinusoidal oscillation earlier in time so displacement is non-zero at t equals zero.

options.label: B
options.text: It increases the maximum amplitude above x₀ while leaving the displacement at t = 0 equal to zero.
options.distractorRationale: The amplitude stays equal to x₀ because sin(ωt + ϕ) stays in [−1, +1]; at t = 0, x(0) = x₀ sin ϕ ≠ 0.

options.label: C
options.text: It doubles the angular frequency of the oscillation and halves the oscillation period.
options.distractorRationale: Phase angle ϕ shifts the waveform horizontally in time without changing ω or period T = 2π/ω.

options.label: D
options.text: It converts the oscillation into a heavily damped decay that stops after one quarter cycle.
options.distractorRationale: Phase angle sets the initial condition of an undamped harmonic oscillation and causes no damping.

items.stem: A block of diamond (refractive index 2.42) touches ethanol (refractive index 1.36). A ray inside the diamond meets the flat boundary at 51° to the normal, with c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Calculate the critical angle for total internal reflection.
items.workedSolution: At the critical angle θ_c, sin θ_c = n₂ / n₁ = 1.36 / 2.42 = 0.5620, giving θ_c = arcsin(0.5620) = 34.2°.

markScheme.criterion: Uses sin θ_c = n₂ / n₁ = 1.36 / 2.42 to obtain θ_c = 34.2° (B).

items.stem: Monochromatic infrared pulses broaden in a wide step-index optical fibre because angled rays travel further than axial rays. How is this modal dispersion reduced?
items.workedSolution: Using a very narrow core (single-mode fibre) forces rays to travel almost axially along nearly identical path lengths. Therefore option C is correct: use a very narrow core so rays travel along nearly identical path lengths.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: use a very narrow core so rays travel along nearly identical path lengths.

options.distractorRationale: White light worsens material dispersion and does not fix modal dispersion.

options.label: B
options.text: To minimise modal dispersion, engineers widen the core diameter so more reflection angles fit inside
options.distractorRationale: A wider core allows steeper oblique rays with larger path differences, worsening modal dispersion.

options.label: C
options.text: To minimise modal dispersion, engineers use a very narrow core so rays travel along nearly identical path lengths

options.label: D
options.text: To minimise modal dispersion, engineers remove the cladding so the fibre is surrounded by air
options.distractorRationale: Replacing cladding with air lowers θ_c, allowing steeper zigzag paths and increasing modal path-length spread.

items.stem: A lightly damped mass-spring system is driven at its natural frequency f₀. What is the phase relationship between the displacement of the oscillator and the periodic driving force?
items.workedSolution: At f = f₀, the driving force acts in phase with oscillator velocity to maximise power input, so displacement lags the driving force by pi/2 rad. Therefore the correct statement is: The oscillator displacement lags the driving force by pi/2 rad (one quarter of a cycle).

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: pi/2 rad.

options.label: A
options.text: The oscillator displacement is completely in phase with the driving force (zero phase lag).
options.distractorRationale: Assumes maximum amplitude occurs when displacement and force peak together rather than velocity and force.

options.label: B
options.text: The oscillator displacement is in antiphase with the driving force, lagging by half a cycle.
options.distractorRationale: Applies the high-frequency asymptotic phase lag instead of the resonance value.

options.label: C
options.text: The oscillator displacement leads the driving force by a quarter of a cycle.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the causal sign of phase lag behind the driver.

options.label: D
options.text: The oscillator displacement lags the driving force by pi/2 rad (one quarter of a cycle).

items.stem: A mass m = 0.9 kg hangs at rest from a vertical spring of stiffness k = 40 N m⁻¹. It is pulled down by x₀ = 0.055 m from equilibrium and released. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Δx_eq = mg / k = (0.9 × 9.8) / 40 = 0.221 m. (b) T = 2π√(0.9 / 40) = 0.942 s. (c) Maximum net SHM acceleration a_max = (k / m) x₀ = 2.44 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mg = k Δx_eq with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Evaluates a_max = ω² x₀ = (k / m) x₀.

items.stem: A 0.4 kg mass oscillates in SHM with angular frequency 10 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 0.1 m. Consider its energy when it passes through displacement x = 0.08 m.

Sets E_p = ½E_tot to obtain x = x₀ / √2.

items.stem: A 2400 m step-index optical fibre has n_core = 1.55 and n_clad = 1.47. Its flat end sits in air (n_ext = 1.00), with a guided ray shown at 17.7°. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) t_axial = n_core L / c = (1.55 × 2400) / 3.00 × 10⁸ = 1.24 × 10⁻⁵ s. (b) Longest guided ray has path L / sin θ_c = L n_core / n_clad, giving t_max = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 1.31 × 10⁻⁵ s. (c) Modal pulse delay Δt = t_max − t_axial = 6.75 × 10⁻⁷ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses t_axial = n_core L / c with n_core = 1.55 and L = 2400 m.
Applies L_max = L (n_core / n_clad) to find t_max = t_axial (n_core / n_clad).

items.stem: A 350 m step-index optical fibre has core index 1.57 and cladding index 1.46. A laser ray in air (n_ext = 1.00) enters the flat end at θ_in = 20.8° to the axis. What angle of incidence θ_w does the ray make with the normal at the core–cladding wall?
items.workedSolution: At the entry face, 1 sin 20.8° = 1.57 sin θ_axis ⇒ θ_axis = 13.1°. Since the core wall is parallel to the axis, its normal is perpendicular to the axis, giving θ_w = 90° − θ_axis = 76.9°.

items.stem: A narrow light ray of vacuum wavelength 405 nm travels through zircon (n₁ = 1.92). It meets a smooth crown glass surface (n₂ = 1.52) at 30° to the normal. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Inside crown glass, v₂ = c / n₂ = 1.97 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and λ₂ = λ₀ / n₂ = 405 / 1.52 = 266 nm. (b) By Snell's law, sin θ₂ = (1.92 sin 30°) / 1.52, giving θ₂ = 39.2°. (c) Angular deviation δ = |θ₂ − θ₁| = 9.17°.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains λ₂ = 266 nm (with v₂ = 1.97 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹).
Substitutes n₁ = 1.92, θ₁ = 30°, and n₂ = 1.52 into n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

items.stem: Each glass core in a coherent endoscope bundle is surrounded by thin cladding of lower refractive index. Which statement best explains why this cladding is essential?
items.workedSolution: Without cladding, contacting glass cores would allow light to cross into neighbouring fibres; lower refractive index cladding ensures total internal reflection and prevents cross-talk.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that lower refractive index cladding ensures total internal reflection and prevents cross-talk.

options.text: Cladding increases the refractive index outside the core so light refracts smoothly into neighbouring fibres.
options.distractorRationale: Higher cladding index would destroy total internal reflection and blur the image.

options.label: B
options.text: Cladding absorbs all light striking the core wall so only rays parallel to the axis reach the camera.
options.distractorRationale: Cladding enables lossless total internal reflection rather than absorption.

options.label: C
options.text: The lower refractive index cladding ensures total internal reflection and prevents cross-talk between adjacent fibres while protecting the core surface from scratches.

options.label: D
options.text: Cladding converts ultraviolet photons into visible light along the length of the endoscope.
options.distractorRationale: No fluorescence occurs in standard step-index cladding.

items.stem: An object of height 0.036 m sits 0.27 m in front of a concave lens of focal length −0.15 m. Calculate the signed linear magnification m = h_i / h_o = −v / u.
items.workedSolution: With f = −0.15 m, 1/v = −1/0.15 − 1/0.27 gives v = -0.0964 m. Therefore m = −v / u = −(-0.09643) / 0.27 = 0.357 (upright and diminished).

markScheme.criterion: Finds v = -0.0964 m and m = −v / u = 0.357 (B).

items.stem: A load of mass m = 0.6 kg hangs at rest from a vertical spring (k = 25 N m⁻¹). It is pulled downwards by x₀ = 0.024 m and released. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Δx_eq = mg / k = (0.6 × 9.81) / 25 = 0.235 m. (b) T = 2π√(0.6 / 25) = 0.973 s. (c) Maximum net SHM acceleration a_max = (k / m) x₀ = 1.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mg = k Δx_eq with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
Evaluates a_max = ω² x₀ = (k / m) x₀.

items.stem: An HL oscillator obeys $x = x_0 \sin(\omega t + \phi)$ with amplitude $x_0 = 8.00\text{ cm}$, angular frequency $\omega = 5.00\text{ rad s}^{-1}$, and phase angle $\phi = 1.05\text{ rad}$ ($\pi/3$).
items.workedSolution: (a) $x(0) = 6.93 cm$. (b) $x(0.200) = 7.11 cm$. (c) $v(0.200) = −0.183 m s⁻¹$. (d) a positive phase angle phi in radians shifts the sinusoidal oscillation earlier in time so displacement is non-zero at t equals zero.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates total phase ωt + ϕ = 2.047 rad in radians.
Applies v = ωx₀ cos(ωt + ϕ) with x₀ = 0.0800 m.
States curve shifts leftwards (earlier in time) by ϕ/ω.
Notes non-zero initial displacement (a positive phase angle phi in radians shifts the sinusoidal oscillation earlier in time so displacement is non-zero at t equals zero).

items.stem: A straight 60 m step-index optical fibre has core refractive index 1.62 and cladding refractive index 1.51. A laser ray in air (refractive index 1.00) enters the flat end at 19.4° to the axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) θ_c = arcsin(1.51 / 1.62) = 68.8°. (b) Using n_ext sin θ_max = √(n_core² − n_clad²) gives θ_max = 35.9°. (c) For θ_in = 19.4°, θ_axis = 11.8° and L_ray = 60 / cos θ_axis = 61.3 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies 1 sin θ_max = n_core sin(90° − θ_c).
Finds θ_axis = 11.8° and evaluates L / cos θ_axis.

items.stem: An object oscillates in SHM with amplitude x₀ = 0.06 m and angular frequency ω = 8 rad s⁻¹. Calculate its speed when x = 0.03 m.
items.workedSolution: Using v = ω√(x₀² − x²) gives v = 8 × √(0.06² − 0.03²) = 0.416 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into v = ω√(x₀² − x²) to obtain 0.416 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: A 1.5 kg block on a smooth table is attached to a horizontal spring of constant 160 N m⁻¹. It oscillates with amplitude 0.075 m. What is the natural frequency f of the oscillation?
items.workedSolution: Natural frequency f = (1 / 2π)√(k / m) = (1 / 2π)√(160 / 1.5) = 1.64 Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Swaps k/m and m/k, computing (1 / 2π)√(m / k) instead of (1 / 2π)√(k / m).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Reports angular frequency ω = √(k / m) in rad s⁻¹ without dividing by 2π.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the period T = 2π√(m / k) instead of frequency f = 1 / T.

items.stem: A flat, parallel-sided zircon plate of thickness 0.05 m and refractive index 1.92 sits in air (n₀ = 1). A light ray meets the entry face at 44° to the normal.
items.workedSolution: (a) Snell's invariant n₀ sin θ₀ = 1 sin 44° = 0.695 (emergent angle = 44°). (b) Inside the slab, θ₁ = arcsin(0.6947 / 1.92) = 21.2°, so Δy = 0.05 tan θ₁ = 0.0194 m. (c) Perpendicular lateral displacement d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0208 m.

Applies d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ or (t₁ tan θ₀ − Δy) cos θ₀.

parts.prompt: State the emergent angle of refraction in air and calculate the optical Snell invariant n₀ sin θ₀.
workingSteps: Because both outer media have refractive index 1 and the faces are parallel, the emergent angle equals 44°.
Snell invariant = n₀ sin θ₀ = 1 × sin 44° = 0.695.

parts.prompt: Calculate the transverse offset Δy = t₁ tan θ₁ of the ray between the entry normal and exit normal along the slab face.
Hence calculate the perpendicular lateral displacement d between the emergent ray and the original incident ray line.
workingSteps: d = (t₁ tan θ₀ − Δy) cos θ₀ = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0208 m.

items.stem: Light travels inside sapphire (n₁ = 1.77) and meets a flat boundary with water (n₂ = 1.33) at 65° to the normal. Take the speed of light in a vacuum as c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) sin θ_c = 1.33 / 1.77, so θ_c = 48.7°. (b) Because n₁ > n₂ and θ₁ > θ_c, total internal reflection occurs at the interface. (c) Wave speed v₁ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.77 = 1.69 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and angular deviation δ = 180° − 2(65°) = 50.0°.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into sin θ_c = n₂ / n₁ = 1.33 / 1.77.
States total internal reflection because the ray is in the higher-index medium with incident angle greater than the critical angle.

State and explain the optical phenomenon that occurs when this beam meets the boundary.
parts.expectedAnswer: Total internal reflection occurs because light travels in the medium of higher refractive index and the incident angle exceeds the critical angle.
workingSteps: Compare incident angle with critical angle in the optically denser medium to confirm total internal reflection.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular deviation of the reflected ray from the incident ray's original forward direction, and find the wave speed in the first medium.
workingSteps: Wave speed in sapphire: v₁ = c / n₁ = 1.69 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
Angular deviation under total internal reflection: δ = 180° − 2(65°) = 50.0°.

items.stem: A 0.4 kg pendulum bob hangs on a 1.6 m wire and swings in SHM with arc amplitude 0.352 m. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the maximum speed v_max of the bob?
items.workedSolution: Angular frequency ω = √(g / L) = √(9.81 / 1.6), so maximum speed v_max = ω x₀ = 0.872 m s⁻¹.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes ω² x₀ = (g / L) x₀ (maximum acceleration) instead of ω x₀ = √(g / L) x₀.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts g / L inside √(g / L) when computing ω x₀.

options.label: A

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes average speed 4A/T over a full cycle instead of peak speed ωA.

items.workedSolution: (a) $\Delta t = (Ln_1/c)(n_1/n_2 - 1) = 891 ns$. (b) use a very narrow core so rays travel along nearly identical path lengths.

workingSteps: Axial time $t_{\min} = L n_1 / c = 1.29 × 10⁻⁵ s$.

items.stem: A heavily damped vibrating beam has undamped natural frequency f₀ = 15.0 Hz and damping ratio ζ = 0.62. Calculate its shifted resonance peak frequency from f_peak = f₀ √(1 − 2ζ²).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Drops the factor of 2 inside the square root.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the square root completely.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies f₀ directly by ζ.

items.stem: A damped torsion pendulum loses amplitude exponentially so each peak is 0.70 times the previous peak. Calculate the percentage of total mechanical energy transferred to thermal energy per oscillation.
items.workedSolution: Since E ∝ A², energy fraction retained = 0.70² = 0.49; percentage dissipated = (1 − 0.49) × 100% = 51.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Treats mechanical energy as linearly proportional to amplitude.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Quotes the amplitude ratio directly.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Applies an erroneous factor of one-half during algebraic rearrangement.

items.stem: A 0.2 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of constant 100 N m⁻¹. It oscillates vertically in SHM with amplitude 0.032 m, where g = 9.8 m s⁻². Calculate the static equilibrium extension Δx_eq of the spring.
items.workedSolution: At static equilibrium, upward spring tension balances weight: k Δx_eq = mg ⇒ Δx_eq = (0.2 × 9.8) / 100 = 0.0196 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides mass m directly by spring constant k without multiplying by gravitational field strength g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds the oscillation amplitude x₀ to mg / k, finding maximum total stretch rather than static equilibrium extension.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Hooke's law as k / (mg) instead of mg / k.

items.stem: A 0.8 kg mass oscillates in SHM with angular frequency ω = 20 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude x₀ = 0.06 m. What is its kinetic energy E_k at displacement x = 0.048 m?
items.workedSolution: Using E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) gives E_k = 0.5 × 0.8 × 20² × (0.06² − 0.048²) = 0.207 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the total mechanical energy ½mω²x₀² instead of subtracting potential energy at x.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the potential energy ½mω²x² at x rather than the kinetic energy ½mω²(x₀² − x²).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Interpolates energy linearly as E_tot(1 − x / x₀) instead of quadratically as E_tot(1 − x² / x₀²).

workingSteps: Glass refractive index is greater for shorter-wavelength blue light than red light.
Mirrors reflect all wavelengths at identical angles, eliminating chromatic aberration.

items.stem: An object oscillates in SHM at 5 Hz with amplitude 0.05 m. At one instant it passes through x = 0.0175 m. Calculate its maximum acceleration a_max = (2πf)² x₀.

items.stem: A short light pulse enters a 900 m step-index optical fibre (core index 1.58, cladding index 1.49). The end sits in air (n_ext = 1.00), with a 22.2° ray shown, and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Calculate the modal delay Δt = t_max − t_axial at the exit.
items.workedSolution: Axial transit time t_min = n_core L / c = (1.58 × 900) / (3.00 × 10⁸) = 4.74 × 10⁻⁶ s. At the critical angle sin θ_c = n_clad / n_core, t_max = t_min / sin θ_c = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 5.03 × 10⁻⁶ s. Modal delay Δt = t_max − t_min = 2.86 × 10⁻⁷ s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δt = (n_core L / c)(n_core / n_clad − 1) = 2.86 × 10⁻⁷ s (B).

items.stem: A straight 120 m step-index optical fibre has a core (n_core = 1.54) and cladding (n_clad = 1.45). A narrow laser beam in air (n_ext = 1.00) meets the flat end at θ_in = 15.9° to the axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) sin θ_c = 1.45 / 1.54 ⇒ θ_c = 70.3°. (b) By Snell's law at the end-face, sin θ_axis = (1 sin 15.9°) / 1.54, so θ_axis = 10.2°. (c) Wall incident angle θ_w = 90° − θ_axis = 79.8°, which exceeds θ_c so the ray is guided by TIR.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts θ_axis from 90° to obtain θ_w.

items.stem: A light ray of vacuum wavelength 650 nm travels in sapphire (n₁ = 1.77). It meets a flat ethanol surface (n₂ = 1.36) at 42° to the normal, with c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Find the angle of refraction θ₂.
items.workedSolution: By Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, so sin θ₂ = (1.77 × sin 42°) / 1.36 = 0.8709. Taking the inverse sine gives θ₂ = 60.6°.

markScheme.criterion: Applies n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ to obtain θ₂ = 60.6° (C).

items.stem: A 0.9 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness 25 N m⁻¹. It then oscillates vertically with amplitude 0.024 m, where g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the static equilibrium extension Δx_eq of the spring?
items.workedSolution: At static equilibrium, upward spring tension balances weight: k Δx_eq = mg ⇒ Δx_eq = (0.9 × 9.81) / 25 = 0.353 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides mass m directly by spring constant k without multiplying by gravitational field strength g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds the oscillation amplitude x₀ to mg / k, finding maximum total stretch rather than static equilibrium extension.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Hooke's law as k / (mg) instead of mg / k.

items.stem: A ball bounces elastically on a hard flat floor, while a mass oscillates on a light spring. Why does the mass on the spring perform simple harmonic motion while the bouncing ball does not?
items.workedSolution: The bouncing ball experiences constant downward g in air rather than a restoring acceleration proportional to displacement from equilibrium. Therefore the correct statement is: Simple harmonic motion requires a restoring acceleration directly proportional to displacement from equilibrium and always directed towards equilibrium.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: simple harmonic motion requires a restoring acceleration directly proportional to displacement from equilibrium and always directed towards equilibrium.

options.label: A
options.text: Simple harmonic motion requires constant downward acceleration independent of position throughout the entire cycle.
options.distractorRationale: Constant gravitational acceleration produces parabolic arcs, not SHM; SHM requires acceleration proportional to −x.

options.label: B
options.text: Simple harmonic motion occurs whenever any motion repeats periodically with a constant time period.
options.distractorRationale: Periodicity alone is insufficient; the restoring acceleration must vary linearly with displacement from equilibrium.

options.label: C
options.text: Simple harmonic motion requires a restoring acceleration directly proportional to displacement from equilibrium and always directed towards equilibrium.

options.label: D
options.text: Simple harmonic motion requires acceleration to be maximum at the equilibrium position and zero at maximum displacement.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses SHM kinematics: acceleration is zero at x = 0 and maximum in magnitude at x = ±x₀.

items.stem: An eye examination shows a patient can focus unaided only on objects between 0.160 m and 0.400 m from the eye.
items.workedSolution: (a) Myopia: eyeball too long or eye lens too powerful focusing parallel rays in front of the retina. (b) $P = -2.50 D$. (c) $u = 0.267 m$.

markScheme.criterion: Explains eyeball too long or lens too strong so parallel rays focus in front of retina.

items.stem: Light enters a 300 m step-index optical fibre from air (refractive index 1.00). The fibre has n_core = 1.58 and n_clad = 1.49, with a 14.3° ray shown. Calculate the maximum acceptance angle θ_max in air.
items.workedSolution: At the grazing limit, sin θ_c = 1.49 / 1.58, so inside the core sin θ_axis,max = cos θ_c = √(1 − (n_clad / n_core)²). By Snell's law at the entry face, n_ext sin θ_max = √(n_core² − n_clad²) = 0.5256, giving θ_max = arcsin(0.5256) = 31.7°.

markScheme.criterion: Uses n_ext sin θ_max = √(n_core² − n_clad²) to obtain θ_max = 31.7° (A).

items.stem: A thin converging lens of focal length 0.15 m acts as a simple magnifier for a 0.008 m tall object. It forms an upright virtual image 0.0808 m in front of the lens (v = −0.0808 m in the real-is-positive convention). Find the object distance u.
items.workedSolution: For a virtual image in the real-is-positive convention, v = -0.0808 m. Thus 1/u = 1/f − 1/v = 1/0.15 − (1/-0.08077) = 19.05 m⁻¹, giving u = 0.0525 m.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes negative v = -0.0808 m into 1/u = 1/f − 1/v to obtain u = 0.0525 m (C).

items.stem: A parallel-sided crown glass plate (thickness 0.06 m, refractive index 1.52) is placed in air (n₀ = 1). A light ray strikes the first face at 44° to the normal. Find the lateral shift d of the emerging parallel ray.
items.workedSolution: By Snell's law, sin θ₁ = (1 sin 44°) / 1.52 ⇒ θ₁ = 27.2°. The perpendicular lateral displacement of the emergent ray is d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0195 m.

items.stem: A light ray in sapphire (n₁ = 1.77) meets a flat boundary with air (n₂ = 1) at 43° to the normal. The speed of light in a vacuum is 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Find the critical angle θ_c between these two media.
items.workedSolution: At the critical angle θ_c, sin θ_c = n₂ / n₁ = 1 / 1.77 = 0.5650, giving θ_c = arcsin(0.5650) = 34.4°.

markScheme.criterion: Uses sin θ_c = n₂ / n₁ = 1 / 1.77 to obtain θ_c = 34.4° (B).

Uses T_cord = mg + mv_max² / L at the bottom of the arc.

items.stem: A step-index optical fibre has core refractive index $n_1 = 1.54$ and cladding refractive index $n_2 = 1.46$. Calculate the critical angle $\theta_{\text{c}}$ at the core–cladding boundary.
items.workedSolution: $\sin\theta_{\text{c}} = n_2 / n_1 = 1.46 / 1.54 = 0.9481$, so $\theta_{\text{c}} = 71.5 °$. Option B (71.5 °) matches.

items.stem: A mechanical oscillator is driven sinusoidally across a range of frequencies. How does the amplitude-frequency response curve change when the degree of damping is increased from light to heavy?
items.workedSolution: Greater damping removes more energy per cycle, so peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak broadens, and the peak frequency shifts slightly below the natural frequency. Therefore the correct statement is: The peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak broadens, and the peak frequency shifts slightly below the natural frequency

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak broadens, and the peak frequency shifts slightly below the natural frequency.

options.label: A
options.text: The peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak narrows, and the peak frequency shifts slightly above the natural frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses both peak broadening and the leftward shift of the damped resonant frequency.

options.label: B
options.text: The peak amplitude decreases, the resonance peak broadens, and the peak frequency shifts slightly below the natural frequency

options.label: C
options.text: The peak amplitude decreases only near resonance while the peak frequency stays fixed at the natural frequency for all damping levels.
options.distractorRationale: Overlooks that damping lowers amplitude at all non-zero frequencies and shifts the peak slightly below f₀.

options.label: D
options.text: The peak amplitude increases slightly at low frequencies while the resonance peak shifts above the natural frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses increased energy dissipation with constructive amplification.

items.stem: A lightly damped pendulum starts swinging with initial amplitude 80 mm and period 1.5 s. During each complete oscillation its amplitude falls to 0.85 of its previous peak. What is its amplitude after 4 complete cycles?
items.workedSolution: Exponential damping multiplies amplitude by r each cycle: A₄ = 80 × (0.85)⁴ = 41.8 mm.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Applies linear amplitude subtraction instead of exponential geometric decay.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies only 3 decay intervals instead of 4.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes amplitude after a single oscillation only.

items.stem: A 0.2 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness 40 N m⁻¹. It oscillates vertically with amplitude 0.024 m about equilibrium. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Δx_eq = mg / k = (0.2 × 9.8) / 40 = 0.0490 m. (b) T = 2π√(0.2 / 40) = 0.444 s. (c) Maximum net SHM acceleration a_max = (k / m) x₀ = 4.80 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mg = k Δx_eq with g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Evaluates a_max = ω² x₀ = (k / m) x₀.

items.stem: A 0.25 kg mass oscillates in SHM with angular frequency 15 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 0.06 m. Consider its energy when it passes through displacement x = 0.036 m.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes m = 0.25 kg, ω = 15 rad s⁻¹, and x₀ = 0.06 m into E_tot = ½mω²x₀².
Applies E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) or E_tot − ½mω²x².
Sets E_p = ½E_tot to obtain x = x₀ / √2.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total mechanical energy E_tot of the oscillating mass.
Calculate the kinetic energy E_k of the mass when its displacement is x = 0.036 m.
workingSteps: E_k = E_tot − E_p = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) = 0.0648 J.

items.stem: A Cassegrain reflecting telescope removes on-axis spherical aberration and directs starlight through a central hole. Which pair of mirror shapes does it use?
items.workedSolution: A Cassegrain reflector uses a concave parabolic primary mirror and convex secondary mirror so on-axis rays focus sharply behind the primary mirror without spherical aberration.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that concave parabolic primary mirror and convex secondary mirror.

options.distractorRationale: A spherical primary introduces spherical aberration and a plane secondary is Newtonian rather than Cassegrain.

options.label: B
options.text: A concave parabolic primary mirror and convex secondary mirror.

options.label: C
options.text: A convex parabolic primary mirror and a concave secondary mirror.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the mirror curvatures; a convex primary would diverge incoming parallel starlight.

options.label: D
options.text: A concave parabolic primary mirror and a concave spherical secondary mirror.
options.distractorRationale: A Cassegrain secondary mirror is convex to increase effective focal length before passing through the primary hole.

items.stem: An object oscillates in SHM at frequency f = 1.5 Hz with amplitude x₀ = 0.03 m. Consider the instant when its displacement from equilibrium is x = 0.0135 m.

items.stem: Narrow laser pulses enter a 360 m step-index optical fibre from air (n_ext = 1.00, ray shown at 9.9°). The core refractive index is 1.5 and the cladding refractive index is 1.44. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) t_axial = n_core L / c = (1.5 × 360) / 3.00 × 10⁸ = 1.80 × 10⁻⁶ s. (b) Longest guided ray has path L / sin θ_c = L n_core / n_clad, giving t_max = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 1.88 × 10⁻⁶ s. (c) Modal pulse delay Δt = t_max − t_axial = 7.50 × 10⁻⁸ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses t_axial = n_core L / c with n_core = 1.5 and L = 360 m.
Applies L_max = L (n_core / n_clad) to find t_max = t_axial (n_core / n_clad).

items.stem: A narrow light ray of vacuum wavelength 670 nm travels through crown glass (n₁ = 1.52). It meets a smooth sapphire surface (n₂ = 1.77) at 38° to the normal. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Inside sapphire, v₂ = c / n₂ = 1.69 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and λ₂ = λ₀ / n₂ = 670 / 1.77 = 379 nm. (b) By Snell's law, sin θ₂ = (1.52 sin 38°) / 1.77, giving θ₂ = 31.9°. (c) Angular deviation δ = |θ₂ − θ₁| = 6.08°.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains λ₂ = 379 nm (with v₂ = 1.69 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹).
Substitutes n₁ = 1.52, θ₁ = 38°, and n₂ = 1.77 into n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

items.stem: In a flexible medical endoscope, why must the imaging bundle be coherent whereas the illumination bundle can be non-coherent?
items.workedSolution: In medical endoscopy, a coherent fibre bundle preserves spatial order of fibres to form an image: each fibre occupies the exact same relative coordinates at the distal and proximal ends.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that coherent fibre bundle preserves spatial order of fibres to form an image.

options.label: A
options.text: A coherent bundle transmits monochromatic laser light only, whereas non-coherent bundles carry white light.
options.distractorRationale: Coherence in endoscopy refers to identical geometric arrangement of fibre ends, not optical phase coherence.

options.label: B
options.text: A coherent fibre bundle preserves spatial order of fibres to form an image without scrambling the scene, whereas illumination only needs to deliver light.

options.label: C
options.text: A coherent bundle removes the need for glass cladding because ordered fibres cannot leak light.
options.distractorRationale: Even ordered fibres require lower-index cladding to prevent cross-talk between neighbouring cores.

options.label: D
options.text: Non-coherent bundles produce sharper images because fibres cross over to average out optical noise.
options.distractorRationale: Crossing fibres would scramble the image completely.

items.stem: An object of height 0.045 m sits 0.42 m in front of a concave lens of focal length −0.3 m. Calculate the signed linear magnification m = h_i / h_o = −v / u.
items.workedSolution: With f = −0.3 m, 1/v = −1/0.3 − 1/0.42 gives v = -0.175 m. Therefore m = −v / u = −(-0.1750) / 0.42 = 0.417 (upright and diminished).

markScheme.criterion: Finds v = -0.175 m and m = −v / u = 0.417 (C).

items.stem: A mass m = 0.75 kg hangs at rest from a vertical spring of stiffness k = 64 N m⁻¹. It is pulled down by x₀ = 0.024 m from equilibrium and released. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Δx_eq = mg / k = (0.75 × 9.81) / 64 = 0.115 m. (b) T = 2π√(0.75 / 64) = 0.680 s. (c) Maximum net SHM acceleration a_max = (k / m) x₀ = 2.05 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses mg = k Δx_eq with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
Evaluates a_max = ω² x₀ = (k / m) x₀.

parts.prompt: Calculate the static extension Δx_eq of the spring when the mass hangs at rest in equilibrium.
Calculate the period T of the vertical simple harmonic oscillations.
Determine the magnitude of the maximum net acceleration a_max of the mass during the oscillation.

items.stem: A $0.400\text{ kg}$ glider moves in SHM given by $x = x_0 \sin(\omega t + \phi)$. Its amplitude is $x_0 = 10.0\text{ cm}$, $\omega = 6.00\text{ rad s}^{-1}$, and $\phi = 1.05\text{ rad}$. What is the total mechanical energy $E_{\text{T}}$ of the oscillation?
items.workedSolution: Total energy is independent of phase angle: $E_{\text{T}} = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.400)(6.00)^2(0.100)^2 = 0.0720\text{ J} = 72.0 mJ$.

items.stem: An optometrist diagnoses a patient with corneal astigmatism because vertical lines appear sharp while horizontal lines at the same distance appear blurred. What is the structural cause of astigmatism?
items.workedSolution: Astigmatism occurs when the cornea has different radii of curvature in perpendicular planes, so perpendicular planes focus at different distances.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that cornea has different radii of curvature in perpendicular planes.

items.stem: A straight 450 m step-index optical fibre has a core (n_core = 1.57) and cladding (n_clad = 1.46). Its flat end sits in air of refractive index 1.00. A light ray enters at θ_in = 15.9° to the axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) θ_c = arcsin(1.46 / 1.57) = 68.4°. (b) Using n_ext sin θ_max = √(n_core² − n_clad²) gives θ_max = 35.3°. (c) For θ_in = 15.9°, θ_axis = 10.0° and L_ray = 450 / cos θ_axis = 457 m.

markScheme.criterion: Applies 1 sin θ_max = n_core sin(90° − θ_c).
Finds θ_axis = 10.0° and evaluates L / cos θ_axis.

items.stem: A 0.45 kg mass oscillates horizontally on a spring of stiffness 18 N m⁻¹. The oscillation amplitude is 0.06 m. Calculate the period T.
items.workedSolution: For an ideal mass-spring oscillator, T = 2π√(m / k) = 2π√(0.45 / 18) = 0.993 s.

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2π and calculates √(m / k) = 1 / ω.

items.stem: A light ray in air (n₀ = 1) strikes a parallel-sided block of flint glass (n₁ = 1.65, thickness 0.085 m). Its angle of incidence is 32° to the normal, and it exits into air on the far side.
items.workedSolution: (a) Snell's invariant n₀ sin θ₀ = 1 sin 32° = 0.530 (emergent angle = 32°). (b) Inside the slab, θ₁ = arcsin(0.5299 / 1.65) = 18.7°, so Δy = 0.085 tan θ₁ = 0.0288 m. (c) Perpendicular lateral displacement d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0206 m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds θ₁ = 18.7° and applies Δy = t₁ tan θ₁.
Applies d = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ or (t₁ tan θ₀ − Δy) cos θ₀.

parts.prompt: State the emergent angle of refraction in air and calculate the optical Snell invariant n₀ sin θ₀.
workingSteps: Because both outer media have refractive index 1 and the faces are parallel, the emergent angle equals 32°.
Snell invariant = n₀ sin θ₀ = 1 × sin 32° = 0.530.

parts.prompt: Calculate the transverse offset Δy = t₁ tan θ₁ of the ray between the entry normal and exit normal along the slab face.
Hence calculate the perpendicular lateral displacement d between the emergent ray and the original incident ray line.
workingSteps: d = (t₁ tan θ₀ − Δy) cos θ₀ = t₁ sin(θ₀ − θ₁) / cos θ₁ = 0.0206 m.

items.stem: A light ray travels inside diamond (n₁ = 2.42) towards a flat boundary with fused silica (n₂ = 1.46). It strikes the boundary at 46° to the normal. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) sin θ_c = 1.46 / 2.42, so θ_c = 37.1°. (b) Because n₁ > n₂ and θ₁ > θ_c, total internal reflection occurs at the interface. (c) Wave speed v₁ = 3.00 × 10⁸ / 2.42 = 1.24 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and angular deviation δ = 180° − 2(46°) = 88.0°.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into sin θ_c = n₂ / n₁ = 1.46 / 2.42.
States total internal reflection because the ray is in the higher-index medium with incident angle greater than the critical angle.

State and explain the optical phenomenon that occurs when this beam meets the boundary.
parts.expectedAnswer: Total internal reflection occurs because light travels in the medium of higher refractive index and the incident angle exceeds the critical angle.
workingSteps: Compare incident angle with critical angle in the optically denser medium to confirm total internal reflection.

parts.prompt: Calculate the angular deviation of the reflected ray from the incident ray's original forward direction, and find the wave speed in the first medium.
workingSteps: Wave speed in diamond: v₁ = c / n₁ = 1.24 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
Angular deviation under total internal reflection: δ = 180° − 2(46°) = 88.0°.

items.stem: A 0.15 kg pendulum bob hangs on a 1.9 m light string and swings in small-angle SHM. Its arc amplitude is 0.418 m, and g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the tension in the string at the lowest point?
items.workedSolution: With ω = √(g / L) = √(9.81 / 1.9), peak speed v_max = ω x₀ = 0.950 m s⁻¹. At the lowest point, T_cord = m(g + v_max² / L) = 1.54 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_max = ω x₀ and T_cord = mg + mv_max² / L = 1.54 N (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Equates cord tension at the lowest point to static weight mg, ignoring the upward centripetal force mv_max² / L.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the centripetal force mv_max² / L from mg instead of adding it at the bottom of the arc.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the net radial centripetal force mv_max² / L rather than the total cord tension.

items.stem: The three stacked graphs display displacement x, velocity v, and acceleration a against time t for an undamped oscillator starting from +A at t = 0. What is the phase relationship between v and x?
items.workedSolution: For x = A cos(ωt), v = −ωA sin(ωt) = ωA cos(ωt + π/2), so velocity leads displacement by π/2 rad (a quarter period). Therefore the correct statement is: Comparing the top two sinusoidal curves, velocity leads displacement by a quarter of a cycle or pi/2 radians, reaching maximum speed as displacement passes through zero.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: velocity leads displacement by a quarter of a cycle or pi/2 radians, reaching maximum speed as displacement passes through zero.

options.label: A
options.text: Velocity is always in phase with displacement so speed reaches its maximum at the amplitude extremes ±A.
options.distractorRationale: At x = ±A the oscillator stops briefly (v = 0); maximum speed occurs at x = 0.

options.label: B
options.text: Velocity is in antiphase with displacement with a phase difference of pi radians.
options.distractorRationale: Acceleration (not velocity) is in antiphase (π rad) with displacement.

options.label: C
options.text: Velocity oscillates at twice the frequency of displacement so its phase difference changes continuously.
options.distractorRationale: x, v, and a all share the exact same oscillation frequency f; only E_k and E_p oscillate at 2f.

options.label: D
options.text: Comparing the top two sinusoidal curves, velocity leads displacement by a quarter of a cycle or pi/2 radians, reaching maximum speed as displacement passes through zero.

items.stem: The glass core of an optical fibre is coated with glass cladding of lower refractive index. Why is this cladding used instead of bare air?
items.workedSolution: Cladding protects the core from surface scratches, prevents crosstalk between adjacent fibres, and provides a clean lower-index boundary for TIR (also reducing modal dispersion). Therefore option B is correct: protects core from surface scratches prevents crosstalk and provides a lower refractive index boundary.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: protects core from surface scratches prevents crosstalk and provides a lower refractive index boundary.

options.text: The lower-index cladding increases the critical angle to zero degrees so even sharp bends never lose light
options.distractorRationale: A smaller n₂/n₁ ratio lowers θ_c; cladding has higher n than air, which actually raises θ_c and reduces modal dispersion.

options.label: D
options.text: The lower-index cladding eliminates material dispersion completely for white light
options.distractorRationale: Material dispersion depends on wavelength-dependent refractive index inside the core, not cladding protection.

items.stem: Which statement accurately defines mechanical resonance for a lightly damped forced oscillator?
items.workedSolution: At resonance the driving frequency equals the natural frequency giving maximum amplitude and maximum rate of energy transfer from driver to oscillator. Therefore the correct statement is: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency giving maximum amplitude and maximum rate of energy transfer

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: driving frequency equals the natural frequency giving maximum amplitude and maximum rate of energy transfer.

options.label: A
options.text: Resonance occurs when the driving force amplitude equals the weight of the oscillator regardless of frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses force magnitude matching with frequency matching.

options.label: B
options.text: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency is twice the natural frequency so the oscillator never loses energy.
options.distractorRationale: Misidentifies the fundamental resonance condition and implies zero dissipation.

options.label: C
options.text: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency giving maximum amplitude and maximum rate of energy transfer

options.label: D
options.text: Resonance occurs when damping is increased until the oscillator stops moving across all driving frequencies.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses overdamping with resonance.

items.stem: A weighted spring is placed in thick viscous syrup, pulled downwards, and released from rest. Which motion best represents heavy overdamping?
items.workedSolution: In viscous syrup, heavy damping causes the mass to return slowly to equilibrium without oscillating. Therefore, option B is correct.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: slow asymptotic creep back to equilibrium without oscillating.

options.label: A
options.text: The mass undergoes rapid oscillations of rapidly growing period until coming to rest.
options.distractorRationale: Assumes heavy damping still crosses equilibrium multiple times.

options.label: B
options.text: The mass undergoes a slow asymptotic creep back to equilibrium without oscillating

options.label: C
options.text: The mass reaches equilibrium faster than any critically damped oscillator.
options.distractorRationale: Incorrectly assumes stronger drag always reduces return time.

options.label: D
options.text: The mass remains permanently stationary at its release displacement because drag cancels spring tension.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses static friction with velocity-dependent viscous drag (which is zero at zero speed).

items.stem: A 0.6 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness 64 N m⁻¹, where g = 9.8 m s⁻². It is pulled down 0.055 m below equilibrium and released. What is the period T of its vertical SHM?
items.workedSolution: Gravity shifts the equilibrium position without altering effective stiffness k, so T = 2π√(m / k) = 2π√(0.6 / 64) = 0.608 s.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes the oscillation amplitude x₀ into a pendulum-style formula 2π√(x₀ / g) instead of 2π√(m / k).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Incorrectly adds weight mg to spring stiffness k, assuming gravity changes the vertical mass-spring period.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Swaps m/k and k/m inside the square root.

items.stem: The SHM energy graph shows a 0.25 kg mass moving with angular frequency 10 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 0.12 m. Calculate its kinetic energy E_k at displacement x = 0.072 m.
items.workedSolution: Using E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) gives E_k = 0.5 × 0.25 × 10² × (0.12² − 0.072²) = 0.115 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the potential energy ½mω²x² at x rather than the kinetic energy ½mω²(x₀² − x²).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Interpolates energy linearly as E_tot(1 − x / x₀) instead of quadratically as E_tot(1 − x² / x₀²).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the total mechanical energy ½mω²x₀² instead of subtracting potential energy at x.

items.stem: When a star is viewed through a refracting telescope fitted with a single-element glass objective lens, coloured fringes appear around the image. Which physical explanation is correct?
items.workedSolution: Glass has a slightly larger refractive index for shorter wavelengths, causing chromatic aberration because blue light refracts more strongly than red light.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that chromatic aberration because blue light refracts more strongly than red light.

items.stem: A mass moves in SHM with frequency f = 1.5 Hz and amplitude 0.03 m. Its displacement at one instant is x = -0.0135 m. Calculate the signed acceleration a.
items.workedSolution: Angular frequency ω = 2πf = 2π(1.5) = 9.425 rad s⁻¹. By the defining SHM equation, a = −ω²x = −(9.425)²(-0.0135) = 1.20 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ω = 2πf and obtains 1.20 m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: A 1200 m step-index optical fibre has n_core = 1.62 and n_clad = 1.51, in air (n_ext = 1.00). A guided ray is shown entering at 21.6°, and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Find the modal dispersion delay Δt between the slowest guided ray and the axial ray.
items.workedSolution: Axial transit time t_min = n_core L / c = (1.62 × 1200) / (3.00 × 10⁸) = 6.48 × 10⁻⁶ s. At the critical angle sin θ_c = n_clad / n_core, t_max = t_min / sin θ_c = n_core² L / (c n_clad) = 6.95 × 10⁻⁶ s. Modal delay Δt = t_max − t_min = 4.72 × 10⁻⁷ s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δt = (n_core L / c)(n_core / n_clad − 1) = 4.72 × 10⁻⁷ s (B).

items.stem: An 80 m step-index optical fibre has core index 1.49 and cladding index 1.39. A laser ray in air (n_ext = 1.00) enters the flat end at θ_in = 14° to the axis. What angle of incidence θ_w does the ray make with the normal at the core–cladding wall?
items.workedSolution: At the entry face, 1 sin 14° = 1.49 sin θ_axis ⇒ θ_axis = 9.34°. Since the core wall is parallel to the axis, its normal is perpendicular to the axis, giving θ_w = 90° − θ_axis = 80.7°.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Gives the refracted angle θ_axis relative to the fibre axis instead of subtracting from 90° to find the angle to the wall normal.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the external launch angle θ_in from 90° without accounting for refraction at the entry end-face.

items.stem: Light in fused silica (n₁ = 1.46) enters a flat transparent sample at 34° to the normal. Inside the sample, the ray refracts to 54.7° to the normal. Calculate the refractive index n₂ of the sample.
items.workedSolution: Rearranging Snell's law n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ gives n₂ = 1.46 × sin 34° / sin 54.7° = 1.00.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates n₂ = n₁ sin θ₁ / sin θ₂ = 1.00 (C).

items.stem: A simple pendulum of length 0.95 m has a 0.12 kg bob. It swings with a small arc amplitude of 0.057 m, where g = 9.8 m s⁻². Find its period T.
items.workedSolution: For small angles, T = 2π√(L / g) = 2π√(0.95 / 9.8) = 1.96 s (independent of bob mass).

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 1.96 s using g = 9.8 m s⁻² (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Swaps L / g and g / L inside the square root, computing 2π√(g / L).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes the half-period π√(L / g) for a single swing from one extreme to the other rather than a complete cycle.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Incorrectly includes the bob mass m inside the pendulum period equation.

items.stem: A clinician must avoid bending a flexible endoscope beyond its minimum safe bend radius. What optical failure occurs if a fibre is bent too sharply?
items.workedSolution: On the outer wall of a tight curve, rays strike more steeply toward the normal; sharp bending reduces angle of incidence below the critical angle causing light leakage.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that sharp bending reduces angle of incidence below the critical angle causing light leakage.

items.stem: An upright object of height 0.02 m stands 0.3 m in front of a thin diverging lens. Its focal length has size 0.2 m (f = −0.2 m in the real-is-positive convention). What is the signed image distance v?
items.workedSolution: For a diverging lens, f = −0.2 m. Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v gives 1/v = −1/0.2 − 1/0.3 = -8.333 m⁻¹, so v = -0.120 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses negative f = −0.2 m in 1/v = 1/f − 1/u to obtain v = -0.120 m (B).

items.stem: A 0.6 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness 25 N m⁻¹, where g = 9.81 m s⁻². It is pulled down 0.024 m below equilibrium and released. What is the period T of its vertical SHM?
items.workedSolution: Gravity shifts the equilibrium position without altering effective stiffness k, so T = 2π√(m / k) = 2π√(0.6 / 25) = 0.973 s.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Swaps m/k and k/m inside the square root.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Incorrectly adds weight mg to spring stiffness k, assuming gravity changes the vertical mass-spring period.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes the oscillation amplitude x₀ into a pendulum-style formula 2π√(x₀ / g) instead of 2π√(m / k).

items.stem: From the stacked SHM graphs shown, a particle oscillates with amplitude $x_0 = 8.00\text{ cm}$ and time period $T = 1.25\text{ s}$. What is the maximum magnitude of its acceleration?
items.workedSolution: $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{1.25} = 5.03 rad s⁻¹$. Maximum acceleration $a_{\max} = \omega^2 x_0 = (5.03)^2 (0.0800) = 2.02 m s⁻²$.

items.stem: A hypermetropic eye has an unaided near point of 1.25 m and an unaided far point at infinity. The person wears reading glasses prescribed for objects at 0.250 m. What is the furthest distance at which objects stay sharp while wearing these glasses?
items.workedSolution: Lens power is $P = \frac{1}{0.250} - \frac{1}{1.25} = 4.00 - 0.80 = +3.20\text{ D}$, so $f = \frac{1}{3.20} = 0.313 m$. For the relaxed eye ($v = -\infty$), $\frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$, hence the new far point is 0.313 m.

items.stem: An upright object of height 0.018 m sits 0.07 m in front of a thin convex lens of focal length 0.2 m. Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v in the real-is-positive convention, find the signed image distance v.
items.workedSolution: Because u = 0.07 m < f = 0.2 m, 1/v = 1/0.2 − 1/0.07 = -9.286 m⁻¹, giving a signed virtual image distance v = -0.108 m.

markScheme.criterion: Computes 1/v = 1/0.2 − 1/0.07 to obtain signed v = -0.108 m (B).

items.stem: An object oscillates in SHM with amplitude x₀ = 0.1 m and angular frequency ω = 30 rad s⁻¹. Calculate its speed when x = 0.05 m.
items.workedSolution: Using v = ω√(x₀² − x²) gives v = 30 × √(0.1² − 0.05²) = 2.60 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into v = ω√(x₀² − x²) to obtain 2.60 m s⁻¹ (C).
